en: Compiled by Shi Dunlun, *Lunben* (Treatise Text), Volume Eleven, Part Six:
The Stage of Samāhita (4a–5a). Section Nine: Clarifying the Objects of Cognition, which are divided into three parts. The first two stages constitute the essence of the objects; all [of these] are...
Because they have consciousness as their nature,
the next three stages are the objective aspects;
this is due to the difference between the coarse and the subtle.
The latter four stages are the stage of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-bhūmi*).
Because there is no mind that is either associated with or dissociated from meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
their two natures— being easy to know and difficult to know— are established as preceding and succeeding.
The three characteristics, categorized by their coarseness and subtlety, form three grades which constitute the sequence of before and after.
Among the four stages, the presence or absence of concentration and distraction constitutes the sequence.
Regarding the first two, their superiority or inferiority constitutes the sequence of before and after.
The latter two [stages] indicate the sequence of manifestation and concealment.
The following four stages are presented here because they clarify the specific positions.
Among them, the first stage is named *samāhita*.
This is translated as "equipoise" (samāhita).
The older term "samādhi" is a corruption and abbreviation.
Master Ji explains it as follows:
This has seven names.
The first is called *samāhita*.
The commentary explains it as follows:
This means that in the stage of supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi-bhūmi*), being free from dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*),
it is able to induce equanimity,
or it induces what is already equanimous.
Alternatively, because it is induced by equanimity (*samatā*),
it is called the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
As stated in the latter part of this fascicle:
It is not the one-pointedness of mind in the desire realm,
because this [state] is induced by concentration, freedom from regret, joy, and bliss;
thus, "equipoise" (samāhita) is explained by these three meanings.
First, the ability to lead;
second, leading to equanimity;
and third, being induced by the skillful means of equanimity.
The inducer and the induced are both equal.
Second is *samādhi*, which here is translated as "equipoise" (*dengchi*).
The old translation "samādhi" is an error.
"Samāpatti" is another term for it;
this means "equilibrium-attainment" (等至).
The old translation "samāpatti" is a corruption.
The fourth is "dhyāna," which here means "meditative concentration" (靜慮).
The old [translation] "dhyāna-artha" is incorrect.
Some say it is a corruption of "dhāraṇa. Others say it is "cittasyaikāgratā."
This is called "one-pointedness of mind. In the *Zhiduolun* (Tattvasiddhi), "mind" (*citta*) refers to its manifold nature, while *ekāgra* means "one.
In the *Yiqieyinyi* (Ekākṣara-kośa), *eka* means "one."
*Akara* means "realm" (*viṣaya*);
*yun* (云) means "nature" (*svabhāva*).
The old translation, "one mind," is an abbreviation.
Sixth is called śamatha; this is translated as "cessation.
Seventh is called "dwelling in happiness in the present life."
Within the sixty-third [section], the meaning of the one-pointedness of mind in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), namely *śamatha* and its abiding, is explained.
Among these various terms, there are three interpretations for the term "the stage of equipoise" (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
According to the true meaning, all meritorious qualities— whether involving the presence or absence of mind— are present exclusively during the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*),
because the three meanings of *samādhi* apply universally therein.
All states of mental distraction (*vikṣipta*) do not belong to this stage.
The term *samādhi* (concentration) refers to the numerical category of "concentration" (*samāhita*) among the five particular mental objects;
it universally encompasses all states of mind that possess consciousness.
The nature of "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*) applies to both concentrated and non-concentrated states.
As analyzed in the fourfold categorization within the *Śāstra*,
various sūtras and treatises refer to the samādhis of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), and so forth, by name only because these are preeminent. However,
*samāpatti* (attainment) generally refers to the essential nature of all meditative states, whether with or without mind, across all levels of concentration.
In various sūtras and śāstras, those meditative concentrations associated with the five types—such as "direct perception" (pratyakṣa) and so forth—are specifically termed "attainments" (samāpatti).
Dhyāna, however, encompasses both states with and without mental activity, as well as both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava), and both defiled (kliṣṭa) and undefiled (akliṣṭa).
It relies upon the four levels of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and no other levels;
however, various sūtras and śāstras, speaking from the perspective of what is predominant, refer to the qualities of mental purity within the form realm as "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*).
The essence of one-pointedness of mind is precisely meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
because it encompasses both the defiled and the pure;
for one-pointedness of mind is the definition of meditative concentration.
Śamatha occurs only in states of mind, not in mindless states;
only in pure states, not in impure ones;
and only in concentrated states, not in distracted minds.
Abiding in happiness in the present life occurs only in the four fundamental dhyānas and not in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*);
it involves pure and untainted minds, and not distracted states or the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
By means of this meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), all meritorious qualities of both conscious and unconscious states are encompassed.
Because it is universally pervasive and all-encompassing, it is specifically designated by the name "ground" (*bhūmi*).
Master Jing stated that the term *samāhita*— formerly known as *samādhi*— is a corruption of the original language.
Tai [Zhi] said:
"The term *samādhi* was formerly called *samāpatti*, which is a corruption of the original language;
thus, the statements of these two masters are contradictory."
Now, it is said that *samādhi* is identical to *samāpatti*;
this should be understood as Master Ki has explained.
The reason for knowing this is as follows:
This is because the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* speaks of the "five noble wisdom samādhis," while this treatise’s twelfth fascicle refers to them as the "five noble wisdom samādhīs.
Master Wonhyo of Silla stated:
The terms "samādhi" and "samāpatti" differ in both name and meaning.
This is known from the explanation of the concentrations of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in the third fascicle of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
The concentrations of the first three stages are definitively termed *samādhi*;
the concentrations of the subsequent seven stages are termed *samāpatti*.
If these are the same term, there is merely a discrepancy between the translations as to whether they are erroneous or correct.
For what reason, among the translations of a single master, is the same term sometimes called *samādhi* and sometimes called *samāpatti*?
From this, one might conclude that they are different. Now, I say this is not so.
That sutra states that *samādhi* is what is here called *samāhita*, which is translated as "equipoise" (*dingyin*).
That [sutra] calls it *samaya*.
The old translation was "right reception" (zhèngshòu);
the current term is "samādhi," translated as "equipoise" (děngchí).
These two meanings are distinct.
Each of these superior [terms] is named as a concise illustration that mutually reveals the others.
I only fear that Master Xiaō might not distinguish between the two characters *di* (地) and *ti* (提), and thus raise this objection indiscriminately.
Furthermore, I have examined the newly translated ten-fascicle *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
The ten stages are all invariably termed *samādhi*;
this is simply due to differences in the phonetic interpretations of the translators.
Within these stages:
First, the preceding [sections] are established and the subsequent ones follow; subsequently, they are explained through mutual interpretation.
Within this, five gates are first set forth.
Second, the explanation by way of the gates.
Within this, there are again two parts.
First, the verse enumerates the five gates.
Next, the prose sections correspond to the verse text.
Finally, the miscellaneous meanings enter the fifth section, "The Essential Tenets of Various Sūtras.
Within these essential tenets, the characteristics of the dharmas—such as the eight liberations listed below—are explained.
The "Miscellaneous Meanings" (*Saṃkīrṇārtha*) also explains the various miscellaneous meanings found throughout the sūtras;
because it interprets the sūtras as a whole,
it constitutes a single section.
Regarding the gate of formal establishment (*vyavasthāna-mukha*), one understands only dhyāna but not the liberations (*vimokṣa*), meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), or attainments (*samāpatti*).
This is because these three are explained only in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (the "lower" treatise).
Within the explanation according to the gates, there are four [sections].
First, the general heading;
second, the formal establishment;
third, the mental attention and its objects.
Fourth, the explanation of the sūtra.
Since the three and the four are combined for clarification, there are four [sections].
As the general heading indicates, there are two [parts] within it.
First, the four gates are presented;
subsequently, they are explained individually.
The names of the four dhyānas are as previously recorded and explained in the fifth fascicle.
The instances of omission, addition, increase, or decrease are as in [section] sixty-three.
Within the *samādhi* [section], there are eleven gates;
the eleventh is not explained.

Because it is easy [to understand], there is furthermore a detailed explanation according to the stage of the śrāvaka. Regarding the four types of practitioners who cultivate meditative concentration:
First, for the sake of attaining dwelling in happiness in the present life;
second, for the sake of attaining knowledge and vision;
third, for the sake of attaining analytical wisdom.
The fourth is for the attainment of the exhaustion of outflows.
The fifth is noble knowledge,
which refers to the wisdom of one's own being.
The wisdom of the *pudgala*,
the pure wisdom, and the wisdom of the fruit.
The wisdom regarding the signs of entering and emerging from meditative absorption consists of the five noble factors;
four of these constitute dwelling in happiness in the present life.
The fifth consists of the thorough contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the severing of the fetters and bonds of other phenomena.
Regarding "that which has causes and requisites for the noble and correct":
the five factors of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are called "having causes."
The three factors— right view, right effort, and right mindfulness—
are termed "possessors" because these seven limbs serve as the causes for noble right samādhi.
Within meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), there are six doors.
The eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) have already been briefly explained following the explanation of the liberations (*vimokṣa*);
therefore, they will not be explained further here.

Furthermore, in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* and other sections, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are explained as being no different from the liberations, and thus they are not explained separately either.
In this establishment, the first part is general and the latter is specific.
Regarding the phrase "induced by concentration and so forth, by freedom from regret, joy,
and bliss," it means that through the observance of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the mind becomes free from regret.
Because there is no regret, there is joy;
because there is joy, there is happiness;
because there is happiness, one attains concentration.
Therefore, this meditative equipoise does not exist in the desire realm;
nor is there a complete absence of thorough and correct investigation of phenomena within the desire realm.
There are four distinct types [of such investigation].
First, the establishment of the joy and bliss born of seclusion;
second, the establishment of the hindrances and obstructions;
third, the establishment of the factors.
Regarding the four names established for meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
there are three parts in the first section.
First, a scriptural citation is presented as a heading.
Next, following the specific explanation:
later, under the section on "the untainted means" (*anāsrava-upāya*), the Blessed One explains the obstacles regarding the sequence of samādhi and liberation.
The joy and other factors induced by desire demonstrate that which is to be abandoned.
Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) that is realized is called "separation" (*visamyoga*).
Furthermore, the phrase "the five dharmas are perfected through cultivation" indicates the dharmas produced by that transformation of the basis.
Joy (*prāmodya*) has the nature of the feeling of gladness (*saumanasya*);
it is established as distinct from [satisfaction] because it is induced by the absence of regret and consists of a profound and correct celebration.
Pleasure (*sukha*) has the nature of the feeling of bliss (*sukhavedanā*).
Two distinct types of the fruit of bliss are established: that which is induced by the removal of all coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), and that which is induced by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
As stated in the fifth fascicle [of this treatise]:
"The joy and bliss born of seclusion."
However, since both of these sensations are pleasant and are collectively termed "joy" (*prīti*) because they arise from the mind,
this [sūtra] merely speaks of joy that is distinct from [bodily] birth.
Otherwise, the various texts would be inconsistent.
As for the claim that equanimity associated with the desire realm is not mentioned among those to be abandoned:
while it is indeed equanimity associated with the desire realm, it is neither a state of joyful attachment nor one of aversion; therefore, it is not something to be abandoned.
Because it does not lead to the unwholesome and abandons the nature of the unwholesome, it is precisely that which is to be abandoned;
therefore, the explanations differ.
[The opponent] asks:
The completion of the karmic path of killing must necessarily be accompanied by hatred;
since hatred is of a nature that causes distress, how could it coexist with joy?
The commentary explains:
Since the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Decisive Analysis) states that hatred coexists with joy,
there is no contradiction.
"Joyful" refers to those practitioners who, from the very beginning, have been pure in conduct and who contemplate the pure practices cultivated on the stage of the equipment (*sambhāra-bhūmi*).
The intended meaning here is that it is only at the stage of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) that one cultivates meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).

Abiding in the stage of the provisions (*sambhāra-bhūmi*), one cultivates pure conduct; through the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*), one gives rise to freedom from remorse and so forth.

At the time of cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the preliminary remote preparation (*pūrva-saṃbhāra*) that must first be established as purity of ethics is called the "stage of provisions."
It is not necessary to enter a formal meditative state (*samāpatti*) before practicing *samādhi*.
Among the explanations that resolve preceding objections and difficulties,
there are three different sūtras.
First, samādhi is taught first and liberation (vimukti) afterwards;
second, liberation is taught first and samādhi afterwards;
third, both are taught simultaneously.
In the passages cited above, after first explaining liberation from the five unwholesome dharmas, the subsequent cultivation of the five dharmas was followed by the explanation of samādhi;
this contradicts the second sūtra.
Therefore, I shall now provide an explanation:
herein, the fundamental meditative absorption is termed *samādhi*,
while the abandonment and suppression of the afflictions is termed "liberation."
Because among the untainted states (*anāsrava*), one primarily relies on the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*) to abandon the various afflictions (*kleśa*),
concentration (*samādhi*) is mentioned first and liberation (*vimukti*) is mentioned afterward.
This does not mean that one cannot abandon the afflictions by relying on the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) before subsequently attaining the fundamental stage.
Among the contaminated states, one primarily relies on the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) to first suppress the afflictions by means of six types of mental attention (*manaskāra*);
this is because one enters the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) by means of the seventh, the mental attention of the "result of the culmination of application" (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*).
There is also a seventh mental application (*manasikāra*) which serves as the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) in the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*),
because it is only subsequently that one attains the fundamental dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*).

In this context, it is stated that because one attains the fundamental *samādhi* only after the afflictions have been abandoned through the fruit of the "attention at the culmination of application" (*prayoganiṣṭhā-manasikāra*),
otherwise it would contradict the explanations in the *Abhidharmapada* and other treatises.
The seventh [type of] mental attention (*manasikāra*) occurs in the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*).
Within the context of the "conjunction" (*sahagata*), both the mental attention and the concentration (*samādhi*) are untainted (*anāsrava*).
That which is conjoined with liberation (*vimukti*) severs the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

This refers to when the mental application (manasikāra) that constitutes the culmination of the preparatory stage (prayoga), which was induced by the mental application in the threshold concentration (anāgamya), enters the fundamental concentration; this is termed "within samādhi.
At the same time as this concentration, it is the path of liberation (vimuktimārga) that realizes unconditioned liberation (asaṃskṛta-vimukti).
Therefore, it is said that samādhi is conjoined with liberation;
it is not the case that the concentration occurring simultaneously with the *prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra* (the attention of the culmination of preparation) is called samādhi,
nor is it the case for the samādhis of other uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), and so forth.

This explains that the preliminary application (*sāmantaka*) occurs in the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*), while the uncontaminated path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) arises based on the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*).
The paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) induced by these two both occur within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This [path] that is capable of severing the afflictions is called "conjoined with liberation" (*vimukti-samprayukta*).

It is not the case that the two preceding types of tainted attention (*sāsrava-manasikāra*) which suppress the afflictions are called the "remaining paths of uninterrupted transition" (*anantarya-mārga*);
these are not conjoined with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The path of liberation that is induced also does not enter the fundamental [meditative state].
Regarding the statement that both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are called "preparatory" (*prayoga*):
they are termed "preparatory" because one has not yet attained the fulfillment of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*).
Since it is taught that the abandonment of afflictions constitutes liberation, the "joy born of seclusion" mentioned at the beginning is explained;
by this, the other types of joy, such as that born of concentration, can be understood.
Alternatively, this phrase may refer to the name of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-bhūmi*), which is designated as *samādhi*.
Because this is capable of liberating one from obstacles, it is called "liberation" (vimokṣa).
It is established as a distinct category alongside the three preceding samādhis and the essence of liberation,
because the respective perspectives differ.
Regarding the second section, the establishment of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the characteristics of the hindrances;
second, the explanation of their nutriment and non-nutriment.
In brief, there are two aspects:
first, the presentation of the headings;
second, the detailed explanation.
Within the hindrance of lethargy and drowsiness (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*),
first the individual characteristics are explained separately,
and subsequently the reason for establishing them together as a single hindrance is established.
Not guarding the sense doors and so forth,
as explained in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*,
the mind becomes extremely dull and narrow.
As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,

the explanation of the establishment of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is provided through two successive expositions within the context of the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*).
First, the characteristics of the two are listed and explained;
subsequently, the reasons for establishing them as "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*) are interpreted.
Within these reasons, there are two further sequences.
According to the first interpretation, the two [hindrances] are established as a single *nīvaraṇa* because they share the same object, namely relatives and so forth, and the same locus.
According to the latter interpretation, they are established as a single *nīvaraṇa* because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are similar.
Regarding the distinct explanation of the characteristics of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) in the former [interpretation], there are three periods of time.
The first refers to the time when one was still a layperson.
The second, "By what causes and conditions did I originally leave home at such a young age? refers to the time of initial renunciation.
The last, "Or perhaps due to recollecting what was previously experienced," refers to the period after having left the household life.
The passage concerning the "similar conduct of understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā*) also consists of three parts.

The first part further explains the remorse of the first two periods regarding matters that ought to be done and those that ought not to be done, up to the point of failing to act or acting contrary to what should be done.
Because those who have newly gone forth from the household life may still engage in what should not be done, fail to do what should be done, or perform the opposite of what should be done,
this section first excludes the remorse (*kaukṛtya*) arising from prior actions, and subsequently distinguishes the remorse that arises later.
The second [interpretation] explains the remorse that arises after one has gone forth:
"excluding the remorse and so forth produced by prior regret" means excluding the remorse that arose while still a layperson.
Regarding those who have not yet abandoned this entanglement of remorse:
it refers to those who have not yet abandoned the remorse that arose at the time they first went forth,
and who subsequently give rise again to the remorse of sorrowful attachment.
This arises because one recalls past instances such as frivolous laughter and the like;
furthermore, this is a specific type of *kaukṛtya* (remorse) that occurs after having gone forth.
The two types mentioned above encompass all forms of *kaukṛtya* pertaining to the three preceding periods of time.
In the case of a layperson, remorse may arise regarding its proper object;
it may share the same objective sphere as restlessness (*auddhatya*).

For one who has gone forth, the initial arising of the mental aspect of remorse regarding what is not a proper occasion for its arising is termed "remorse regarding an improper occasion" (*asthāna-kaukṛtya*).
Therefore, the third concluding passage of the treatise states:

"The remorse arising from an improper object immediately preceding [the distraction], as well as the remorse arising at a later time after one has gone forth, although their objective bases are not identical to those of restlessness, are nevertheless similar in character."
It is not only because they share the same object;
remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and longing (*anvaya-śoka*) are established in conjunction with restlessness (*auddhatya*).
After one has gone forth [into the religious life], these two have different objects.
Regret (kaukṛtya) is also established as an *nivaraṇa* because it involves anxiety and longing; however,
while it is not the essential nature of restlessness (*auddhatya*), it does not pervade all defiled minds,
though its activity (*ākāra*) is predominant [in certain cases].
At this time, it does not exist;
because the locus of its description is inconsistent,
it does not contradict the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Regarding the section on doubt:
"Toward the Teacher" refers to the two jewels of the Buddha and the Sangha;
"toward the Dharma" refers to the principle.
The learner practices;
the instructor teaches;
the realized one attains the fruit.
These are the four jewels of Dharma: doctrine, realization, practice, and fruit.
Because one harbors doubts regarding the Three Jewels, one is unable to enter the path of courageous skillful means, the right abandonments, or the truth of cessation which is tranquility.
"Expedient means" refers to the path of application;
"right abandonment" refers to the truth of the path;
and "tranquility" refers to the truth of cessation.
The following clarifies nutriment (*āhāra*) and non-nutriment (*anāhāra*).
Nutriment has the meaning of sustaining and increasing; it is the condition for the growth of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Non-nutriment is the dharma that cuts off and extinguishes the hindrances.
Regarding the phrase "if one can remain detached from defiled minds and so forth," this merely sets forth the reason for focusing on pure and sublime signs.
As for the nine grounds of resentment:
As stated in the fifty-fifth [chapter]:
"The light of the Dharma" refers to a certain person who, according to what they have received, reflected upon, and contacted,
applies the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation respectively.
"Contemplating all phenomena" refers to the three types of wisdom mentioned above.

Furthermore, "realizing contemplation" as that which can counteract torpor, drowsiness, and darkness means that "realization" refers to the cultivation of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
This means that within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the contact between wisdom (*prajñā*) and its object is called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Through the light of the Dharma, the wisdom arising from hearing and reflection removes ignorance and doubt;
while in the stage of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), it is able to remove torpor and drowsiness.
Because it can clearly manifest the nature of all phenomena, it is called the "light of the Dharma.

Regarding its being "non-nutriments," as for the term "laughter," it refers to cases where someone, perhaps due to an expository discourse (*vyākaraṇa*) or a synthetic discourse (*saṃkṣepa-vyākaraṇa*), [experiences such joy].
Speaking openly is called *kārikā* (explanatory discourse).
Speaking cryptically by means of metaphors and then reconciling them to bring about understanding is called *saṃgīti* (reconciliatory discourse).
Opening one's mouth and smiling is called "revealing the teeth."
The sound produced from within the throat is called "ya-ya.
Regarding the nine types of mental abiding (*navavidha-cittasthiti*),
they are explained as in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, fascicle thirty, and the *Abhidharmakośa*, chapter ten, and so forth.
Regarding "that which has conditions" and "dependent origination":
that which has conditions refers to resultant phenomena;
dependent origination refers to causal phenomena.
Within the third section, the establishment of the factors (*aṅga-vyavasthāna*), there are two parts:
first, the establishment of their number based on the stages (*bhūmi*);
second, the explanation of their inclusion and exclusion.
First, the initial explanation of the names:
"aṅga" means a constituent part, as in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) or the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
The Sarvāstivādins explain it thus.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is both meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and a limb of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*);
the others are limbs of meditative absorption but not meditative absorption itself.
Such is the meaning according to reality.
Just as a fourfold army consists of distinct units that counteract one another,

so too do the three factors— equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension— rely upon the state of meditative concentration; because they are equally capable of removing hindrances, they are termed "internal serenity."
Because they purify all hindrances.
The remaining names are easily understood.
As for the discernment of their essence, there are seven.
Because there is the feeling of pleasure in the first and second dhyānas,
and because the essence of internal serenity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) is not faith (śraddhā).
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
Excluding the first dhyāna, the factors of absorption (aṅga) are established within both the remaining two dhyānas.
If these are impure or pure dhyānas, the two types—vitarka and vicāra—are present together with cultivated wisdom (bhāvanāmayī prajñā).
Whenever one cultivates any such merit, vitarka and vicāra are present during the preliminary application (prayoga).
If it reaches the fundamental [dhyāna], there is no vitarka or vicāra.
If it exists within the eightfold path with outflows (sāsrava), the essence of vitarka is established as right thought (samyak-saṃkalpa).
Within the branches of the eightfold path without outflows (anāsrava), if it is associated with subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna), [it is so].
Since right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is established as a frequent occurrence of investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*), giving rise to verbal expression,
the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)— which simultaneously constitutes the eightfold noble path— is explained as being two in terms of its single essence of wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is called right view because it is free from wrong views;
it is called right intention because it is free from wrong intentions.
Since realized wisdom is not caused by verbal expression, right intention is not established based on the substance of that investigation.
Because the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* asks, "For what reason do those with purified awakening and so forth [speak]?
it is known that subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) arises and speaks in association with discursive thought (*vitarka*).
It is taught that the two types—[the wisdom of equality and subsequently attained wisdom]—are of one essence in terms of their joyful aspiration.
If it causes the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to experience a state of mental satisfaction, it is termed joy (*prīti*);
if it causes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the physical body to experience physical satisfaction, it is termed bliss (*sukha*).
This is based on the text of the *Abhidharma*.
If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
that which causes the ālayavijñāna upon which it depends to experience a state of satisfaction is called "pleasure" (*sukha*).
Although the ālayavijñāna is always characterized by the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), [it is so designated because it is satisfied].
Nevertheless, even in the painful realms such as the hells, it causes that which depends upon it to experience no small measure of comfort;
yet in the blissful realms of humans and devas, it causes the ālayavijñāna to be joyful, contented, and secure.
Although it is explained within the context of the first and second dhyānas that joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) both possess the nature of the mental factor of joy (*saumanasya*),
this is done by way of explaining the association between virtues and afflictions and their respective feelings. Thus,
it is stated that the first and second dhyānas are associated with the faculty of joy (*prītīndriya*), but not that they are accompanied by bliss (*sukha*).
Next, regarding the section on refutation and establishment:
first, concerning the determination that vitarka and vicāra take the object of apprehension and so forth,
the Abhidharma explains three [types].
That is to say, vitarka and vicāra serve as the remedy;
joy and bliss serve as the benefit;
and meditative concentration serves as the basis.
Regarding this, four [branches] are taught. Tái says:
"In general, the branches of dhyāna are explained by means of three meanings."
Because the *Abhidharma* subsumes these four under three categories,
it is stated here that the factors (*aṅga*) are briefly of two kinds:
because they provide the benefit of adding gratitude and joy, and so forth, to the practitioner.
If a dharma possesses these two meanings, it is established as a factor of concentration (*samādhi-aṅga*);
since other factors such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and reflection (*vitarka*) lack these two meanings,
they are omitted and not mentioned.
Master Ji said:
"In this context, when vitarka and vicāra are said to take what is to be grasped as their object,
the observation of the appropriate object serves as the antidote."
Concentration serves as the basis;
joy experiences what has been attained;
and bliss removes heaviness and rigidity.
The mental feeling of being appropriately pleased is called joy (*prīti*);
that which can gladden the body is called bliss (*sukha*).
When coarse and heavy states within the body arise and then cease, it is termed tranquility (*praśrabdhi*).
It does not eliminate the lower afflictions;
for the elimination of the lower afflictions occurs solely through vitarka and vicāra.
This clearly demonstrates that the "beneficial factors" (*anuśaṃsa-aṅga*) mentioned in various places have two meanings:
first, the apprehension of the attained object;
second, the removal of the obstacle of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
In the third and fourth dhyānas, the very experience of what has been attained constitutes the removal of the heavy residues (dausthulya);
there is no separate entity,
as they possess both capacities.
Because it brings satisfaction to the faculties by relinquishing coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*),
and because it is superior to other factors present within the various dhyānas,
it is established specifically as a constituent (*aṅga*) for those practicing meditative concentration, owing to its great benefit.
However, as for the detailed analysis of the meaning of these factors of dhyāna,
it shall be explained further in the sixty-third [chapter].
Within the fourth section, "The Establishment of the Names of Samādhi":
First, the specific names will be explained, followed by the general name.
Regarding the first part:
up to the fourth dhyāna, it should be understood that there is the distinction of "purity of equanimity and mindfulness."
Regarding the distinctions in understanding, there are two types of understanding that comprehensively clarify the distinctions among the four dhyānas: namely,
[the state] with vitarka and vicāra, [the state] with the subsiding of vitarka and vicāra,
and [the state] with the subsiding of prīti.

The two explanations clarify the distinctions solely in relation to the third dhyāna, namely: "delight in tranquility" (*praśrabdhi-sukha*) and "purity of equanimity and mindfulness" (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi*).
The third dhyāna also possesses equanimity and mindfulness,
yet it is not called "pure" because one has not yet abandoned the afflictions and other defilements above that level.
In the fourth dhyāna, however, it is pure because the obstacles have been completely eliminated.
Because it is named "attainment of purity through equanimity and mindfulness," one should know that there is a distinction.
Below, the explanation of the general name has five parts.
First, the higher mind;
second, dwelling in happiness in the present life;
third, partial nirvana.
Fourth, the differentiation of nirvāṇa;
fifth, the emergence from all matters of sensation.
The text is divided into four parts.
Because the third and fourth [foundations] are combined through analysis.
Regarding "the mind of higher resolve" (*adhicitta*), the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is termed "mind."
It is because the essence of concentration itself is pure that it is capable of deliberation;
alternatively, it may be because the mental sovereign (citta-rāja) occurring simultaneously with it is pure,
thereby causing those factors of concentration to engage in correct and careful deliberation.
Within the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*),
first there is the understanding of happiness,
and next the understanding of dwelling in the present life.
The subsequent explanation for why the formless realms are not so designated is as follows:
"experiencing joy and bliss" refers to the feeling of joy (*prīti-vedanā*) and the feeling of ease (*sukha-vedanā*).
The bliss of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-sukha*) is the bliss of lightness and ease;
the bliss of equanimity (*upekṣā-sukha*) is the bliss of the feeling of equanimity;
and the bliss that gladdens body and mind is the bliss of delight.
Regarding "dwelling in bliss," sixty-three [authorities] have explained it as follows:
because one binds the mind within so that it does not flow outward, this dwelling—which is capable of inducing bliss—is called "dwelling in bliss.
This is stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
Suffering with outflows (*sāsrava*) is bound to the three realms;
suffering without outflows (*anāsrava*) is comprised within that which is unbound.
Now, based on body and mind together, there are four types of pleasure.

Because they possess the bliss of joy (*prīti-sukha*), the bliss of pleasure (*sukha-sukha*), the bliss of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-sukha*), and the bliss of equanimity (*upekṣā-sukha*), the four dhyānas are termed "abidings in bliss.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the latter two do not exist.
The formless realms lack the first two [dhyānas];
therefore, although pleasure may be present there, it is not called "dwelling in pleasure.
Furthermore, joy and pleasure refer to the pleasure of the first and second dhyānas.
The bliss of the third dhyāna is the bliss of tranquility;
the bliss of the fourth dhyāna is the bliss of equanimity.
The mention of "bliss of body and mind" serves to distinguish this from the non-blissful abiding of the formless realm.
An objection is raised:
"In the fourth [dhyāna], there is the sensation of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā). The sensation of equanimity is called the 'abandonment of pleasure' (upekṣā-sukha)."
Since the four formless attainments possess the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), they should also be called "equanimous bliss. Therefore,
the present explanation states:
That [state] possesses only mental pleasure,
whereas this possesses both physical and mental pleasure;
therefore, only this is called "abiding in pleasure," and not the four formless attainments.
The forest-dwelling bhikṣus then raised a critique, saying: "When I questioned him regarding the peaceful liberation that transcends both form and formlessness, he was unable to provide an answer.
The meaning of this statement is that the meditative absorption of the formless realm (ārūpya-samādhi) is what is meant by "transcending form."
The untainted meditative absorptions (anāsrava-samādhi) are called "transcending the formless" because these two are designated as the "peaceful liberations.
Now, it is explained that the formless absorptions are not for the sake of dwelling in pleasure.
The four dhyānas of the form realm are called the liberations of tranquility;
they are dwellings in happiness in the present life. There is an explanation [to this effect].
Regarding "transcending the realms of form and formlessness":
it is called "transcending" not because of passing beyond external objects, but because of reaching the ultimate limit; therefore, it is called "transcending."
Just as joy (*prīti*) is the limit of the second dhyāna and so forth,

because it is not definitive due to the partial abandonment of various afflictions, it is called "partial nirvāṇa" (*tadaṃśikanirvāṇa*). Here, "one part" refers to pure concentration (*śuddhaka-samādhi*),
untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), and the concentration of relish (*āsvādana-samādhi*).
The abandonment of that attachment to meditative absorption is called "partial nirvāṇa" (*tad-aṃśika-nirvāṇa*) because it constitutes the abandonment of a portion of the various afflictions.
Since it possesses the quality of tranquility, it is termed "nirvāṇa.
Because this [state] is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), subject to rapid movement, and not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), yet it is certain and quiescent regarding doubt, it is designated as partial nirvāṇa.
The essence of the pure and the untainted is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and is not actually *nirvāṇa*.
However, because it is free from afflictions and resembles a small portion of that *nirvāṇa*—though not definitively so—it is called "partial *nirvāṇa*" (*tad-aṃśika-nirvāṇa*).

Alternatively, because a portion of the active afflictions (*samudācāra-kleśa*) within the four pure dhyānas has been severed while their seeds have not, one may later regress and be reborn; because this is not definitive, it is called "partial nirvāṇa" (*tad-aṃśika-nirvāṇa*).
Regarding the statement that it is called "distinctive nirvāṇa" because it is not ultimate:
due to the partial pacification resulting from the abandonment of afflictions, it is conventionally designated as "nirvāṇa," yet it is not ultimate pacification.
Therefore, it is called "distinctive nirvāṇa.
The fifth [section] is titled "Emergence from the Affairs of All Sensations," which contains four parts.
First, the four emergences are stated, followed by citations from the sūtras to establish their validity.
Second, the two [factors] and the five factors of the realm of renunciation mutually subsume one another.
Third, the explanation of the six factors of the realm of renunciation based on the three causes.
Fourth, the explanation that being free from all faults is called the basis of renunciation.
The beginning consists of three parts:
first, the presentation of the four types of renunciation;
second, the explanation of the sūtra on renunciation.
The subsequent section consists of questions and answers for clarification.
There are three meanings of "renunciation" (*niḥsaraṇa*):
first, the meaning of non-practice.
Second is the sense of eliminating coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*);
third is the sense of being free from defilement (*vairāgya*).
The first dhyāna is free from sorrow and possesses these three meanings.
The two concentrations (dhyāna) are free from suffering solely in the sense that they eliminate the heavy residues (dausthulya);
for although defilement has already been abandoned at the initial stage, it still persists subsequently.
The latter three [liberations] possess both the elimination of heavy residues and the sense of being free from defilement.

The state of signlessness and the abandonment through dissociation pertain exclusively to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). In other stages, although there may be dissociation, it cannot be termed "abandonment through dissociation.
Regarding the Sūtra on Liberation, there are two [interpretations].
First, the *Vimilā-sūtra* is explained;
subsequently, other sūtras are treated by analogy.
In this manner, one should understand that the text applies accordingly to the remaining [sūtras] as appropriate.
"One who knows the sequence":
"sequence" refers to the causal basis;
it is that which can bring forth the characteristics.
This refers to the sense faculties, objects, and so forth.
Regarding the seeds of ignorance:
it is because ignorant people give rise to much sorrow.
All of these are termed "introductions.
Even if it is not defiled sorrow, it is still said to arise from delusion (*moha*).
Furthermore, all types of afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of giving rise to sorrow.
Ignorance is the root; it is taught that this seed [of unwholesomeness] arises from the nature of the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya).
Because it is impaired by delusion (moha), it must be abandoned through detachment.
As for the others, they likewise cease following the cessation of ignorance.
If there is discursive thought that is not innate,
it is abandoned even upon the departure from desire,
because the associated categories of the innate faculty of grief are also abandoned.
Within the question-and-answer section, there are three parts:
first, the characteristics of the faculties;
second, the elucidation of the faculty of suffering.
Later, the absence of [the faculty of] suffering will be explained.
Within the first dhyāna, the heaviness (dausthulya) of the faculty of suffering has not yet been abandoned because the faculty of grief lacks meditative equipoise (samāhita).
When one is free from defilement, all [afflictions] do not function and the heavy burdens (dausthulya) are also abandoned.
Even if there is longing, sorrow, or distress regarding the unsurpassed Dharma, there is no cognition that induces them.

Therefore, while the abandonment through the departure from desire arises from the various faculties of suffering, it does not arise from being induced by ignorance; thus, even when free from desire, they may still function.
Therefore, those two types of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) and lack of adaptability (*akarmanyatā*) are only extinguished by the two meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).

Question: The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is abandoned through detachment from desire and is extinguished in the second dhyāna; joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) are abandoned through detachment from the lower [levels], and equanimity (*upekṣā*) arises.
The coarse and heavy [factors] are eliminated in the higher stages.
Answer: Because the basis for the faculty of suffering, as well as vitarka and vicāra, exist in the first dhyāna, these two are extinguished in the second dhyāna.
There is no separate basis for joy and bliss that could be further induced.
When one is free from passion, the coarse and heavy states (*dauṣṭhulya*) perish.

If the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) has already been abandoned in the first dhyāna, then there would be no difference in the experience of abiding for a practitioner entering the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna.
This means that the first dhyāna eliminates sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and the second dhyāna eliminates suffering (*duḥkha*); by virtue of this,
although there is abiding in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), a distinction is nevertheless established.
If suffering had already been extinguished within the first dhyāna,
there would be no distinction between the second dhyāna and other states of dwelling in happiness in the present life;
yet the Sūtra says:
Because the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) differ in their emergence from feeling and in their establishment through differentiation;
furthermore, because there is a distinction in the abandonment of feeling therein.
In the first absorption, applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra) are not yet stilled, and their coarse heaviness (dausthulya) has not been abandoned or extinguished.
Only upon entering the second dhyāna is there tranquility, and only then are the heavy residues (dausthulya) severed and extinguished.
If the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) were already severed within the first dhyāna, this distinction [between the two] would not exist.
Furthermore, regarding those such as the signless (animitta) practitioners...
Jingyun: For one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the untainted meditative mind that takes true suchness (*tathatā*) as its object is called "signless" (*animitta*).

The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) associated with afflictions is either mixed with afflictions or bound by them as their conditions; both are the heavy obstructions (*dauṣṭhulya*) upon the very substance of the faculty of equanimity.
Now it is explained that the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) which bind the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are called "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*).
To extinguish those seeds of affliction within the signless concentration (*ānimittasamādhi*) is called "extinguishing the latent tendencies.
This does not mean extinguishing the currently experienced [feeling] that is termed the faculty of equanimity.
Because there must necessarily be feeling within the concentration of signlessness (animitta-samādhi),
and because feeling is not by nature an affliction (kleśa),
the seeds of various feelings are not termed latent dispositions (anuśaya).
Therefore, it is said that those various feelings do not possess latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Rather, because the afflictions taking neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*) as their object are abandoned, it is said that neutral feeling is abandoned.
The heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the category of those afflictions is what is designated by the term "latent disposition."
Tài said: "When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) practices the contemplation of emptiness, they grasp at signs and abandon the seeds of the faculties, which are then eternally extinguished.
The latent tendencies (anuśaya), like stiff silk floss, are called 'coarseness' (dauṣṭhulya)."
It is called the cessation of active manifestation because the coarse and heavy [afflictions] are abandoned without remainder. Why?
Because one who dwells in the concentration on signlessness must necessarily relinquish the grasping of signs.
Now, as for abandoning the designation of "latent dispositions" (*anuśaya*) for the seeds of currently active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*),
this is done because it is spoken of according to their names;
it is not that those who delight in various feelings possess coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) as latent dispositions.
It is called "abandonment" because one abandons those various afflictions;
the seeds of the various feelings belonging to the category of those afflictions are termed "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*). Ji says:
The seeds of impure equanimity, bound by afflictions, are conventionally designated as "coarseness" (dauṣṭhulya);
upon entering this meditative absorption, these are said to be severed.
The active manifestation of pure equanimity is conventionally designated as "active entanglement" (paryavasthāna), which continues to arise even while one remains in the absorption.
It is not that those various feelings themselves are defiled by afflictions such that they possess latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); rather,
it is these very latent dispositions that are termed "gross heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*).
It is not that uncontaminated feeling lacks seeds;
there is an explanation that this refers to those who have not yet extinguished the manifest entanglements.
It is not the substance of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) that is bound by the fetters and afflictions associated with cessation;

rather, this refers to the act of taking up the faculty of equanimity—which is bound—along with the corresponding afflictions and so forth, and designating it as "active entanglement" (*paryavasthāna*).
This does not mean that these present fetters are extinguished.
Furthermore, while this faculty of equanimity actually extends across nine stages,
it is here described as being in five stages based on those levels where it exists exclusively as equanimity.
The second section, concerning the mutual inclusion between [the factors] and the five realms of renunciation (*pañca-nairyāṇika-dhātu*), consists of three parts:
first, restating and explaining the term "renunciation";
second, resolving objections.
Third, regarding the *Miśrakābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*:
it states that from the renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*) of desire, ill-will, and harmfulness, up to the renunciation of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Here, the renunciation of initial desire refers to the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Next, renunciation of ill-will is the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Finally, renunciation of harmfulness is the contemplation of compassion (*karuṇā*).
These three forms of renunciation constitute the renunciation of the four faculties of sorrow, suffering, joy, and happiness.
Because loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) are attained through all four dhyānas,
within the fourth dhyāna, loving-kindness and compassion are the transcendence of the four feelings (*vedanā*).
Since they are a transcendence of form (*rūpa*), it is said that they are the transcendence of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) in the fourth dhyāna.
This attainment of the concentration of the sphere of infinite space is the renunciation of the faculty of equanimity from the four dhyānas, because it is free from desire for form.
Regarding "by the cessation of the view of a self-existent body" (*satkāya-nirodha*):

this refers to the moment when the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*), free from the defilements of the three realms, reaches its final exhaustion; at that time, it is said that the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) emerges from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
These latter two types are collectively termed the "equanimity of renunciation" (*niḥsaraṇopekṣā*).
What is the meaning of the term "conducive to renunciation" (*naiṣkramya-saṃprayukta*)? Because one who dwells in this [state] is able to renounce, it is called "conducive to renunciation.
One who dwells in this contemplation is an *aśaikṣa* (one beyond training); because they accord with this contemplation, it is termed "conducive to renunciation."
It is not said that one departs from those [afflictions] by means of this;
that is to say, it is not said that ordinary persons or those in training depart from greed, hatred, and harmfulness through these five contemplations.
It is said that this realm is taught for the sake of those who seek to be free from desire.
These five kinds of realms conducive to renunciation are taught for those who have already become free from desire for the three realms.
Regarding the resolution of objections,
as for the phrase "although those various forms of renunciation are simultaneous," etc.:
Although desire, ill-will, and harmfulness are abandoned simultaneously,
three distinct antidotes are established for them based on their respective preliminary applications. Furthermore,
three modes of renunciation are established based on the cultivation of three distinct contemplations by three types of individuals.
Regarding those three types of persons whose afflictions increase predominantly, each practices a specific contemplation— either loving-kindness (*maitrī*) or compassion (*karuṇā*)—
and is thereby able to transcend desire, ill-will, and harmfulness.
Since there is only one category of antidote for what follows [the third stage], there is no distinction in their subsequent transcendence.
The fourth [counteractive] is the class of antidotes that, distinct from the departure from form, contemplates all forms as empty based on the sphere of infinite space.
The fifth is the class of antidotes that separately cultivates the untainted contemplation of emptiness regarding the body of the four aggregates.

The treatments for the preceding and succeeding [stages] are distinct; they do not differ from the three preceding [cases] in that they emerge simultaneously, nor are they differentiated into many parts.
Therefore, it is said that there is no distinction.
Regarding the question, "What is meant by those with sharp vision? and so forth, the subsequent commentary contains twenty-eight phrases.
The first thirteen phrases concern the path of skillful means for abandoning desire;
the latter fifteen phrases, which are the opposite of these, concern the actual path for abandoning desire.
The intention of this sūtra is to reveal that through the aforementioned preparatory practice followed by the path of detachment,
the defiled sensations do not arise in the body of an Arhat, and the various afflictions do not manifest,
just as water droplets do not adhere to a red lotus.
Thus, performing the five reflections is called "conforming to renunciation.
Within the first thirteen phrases,
the first phrase is a general designation for the person, referring to one who possesses sharp insight.
Next, the twelve phrases provide a detailed explanation of that contemplation.
Regarding the first [phrase], "by means of the contemplative attention of investigation":
among the seven types of attention, this refers to the "attention of investigation"; this term serves as a general designation.
"Attention directed toward superior matters" explains the desire for recollection of the qualities [of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha].
"Attention characterized by intense effort" explains the one with intense vision.
How, then, are the twelve phrases individually explained regarding the various desires?
The first eight phrases concern the contemplation of non-attachment to desire, while the latter four phrases concern the contemplation of revulsion toward desire. Question:

Why does the text mention only the mental application of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-manasikāra*) and not explain the mental application of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manasikāra*) and the others?
Master Ji says:
"It is now stated that because the Arhat, having ultimately abandoned desire for the three realms, performs five kinds of contemplation—
namely, the attention of the culmination of the preparatory application (prayoga-niṣṭha-manasikāra) for abandoning the defilements of the formless realm."

Since the preceding path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) consists of the mental application of observation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*), according to this principle, the subsequent passage within the path of right abandonment (*samyak-prahāṇa-mārga*) explains "the mind being well-gone" (*citta-sugata*) by referring to the mental application of the culmination of preparation (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-manasikāra*).
What is meant by "abiding"? It refers to abiding in the mental application of the culmination of preparation.
In the subsequent fifteen phrases,
the four [factors] beginning with "mental engagement and entry" each reverse the preceding ones;
the textual characteristics are easily understood.
This refers to one who abides in the attention that culminates the application;
it is the attention that culminates the abandonment of the defilements of the formless realm.
At this time, one correctly abandons all afflictions.
One who has attained the ultimate path of the sublime mind is called a Sugata;
this refers to one who has skillfully cultivated other modes of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
This refers to having well-cultivated the aforementioned mental attentions (*manasikāra*) such as investigation.
Master Jing interprets "the rest" as referring to the five preceding types of mental attention.
This explanation concerns the stage of abandonment (*prahāṇa*) as well as the stage of the path of preparation for abandonment (*prahāṇaprayoga-mārga*).

This refers to the summary statement that reveals the stage of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) where the mental application of the culmination of preparation (*prayoga-niṣṭha-manasikāra*) effects abandonment,
as well as the stage of the path of means (*upāya-mārga*) where the mental application of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*) and others effect abandonment.
"Liberation" (*vimukti*) refers to the liberation from the fetters of the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*).
"Liberation" (vimukti) refers to liberation from the bonds of manifest activity (paryavasthāna). Both of these are instances of active manifestation.
"Disentanglement" (visaṃyoga) refers to being free from the bondage of the seeds (bīja) of the aforementioned two types of bonds.
Regarding the outflows (*āsrava*) arising from the conditions of various desires,
those involving sensual greed (*kāmarāga*) are excluded because they have already been thoroughly loathed during the preceding stage of preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*).
As for "impairment" (*upaghāta*):
The "woeful realms" (durgati) are called "damage" (hāni). Being "destitute of virtuous fruits" (kuśalaphala) is called "privation" (vighāta).

Regarding liberation from them—transcending and becoming dissociated—it means, as previously stated in sequence, being liberated from the envelopments (paryavasthāna), their objects (ālambana), and the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
Master Ji said:
"To be liberated from the fetters is called 'transcending' (chao);
to be liberated from the objects of perception is called 'emerging' (chu)."
Liberation from the latent tendencies (anuśaya) is called dissociation (visamyoga). Now,
to explain "in that regard":
This refers to what was previously described as outflows (*āsrava*), deprivation (*pariśūnya*), burning afflictions (*paridāha*), and so forth.
Liberation (*vimukti*), transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*), and dissociation (*visaṃyoga*) follow the same sequence as before.

Being freed from the signs of the object of focus is called "transcending";
being liberated from latent tendencies is called "disjunction.
This refers to relying on the recollection of various objects of desire, whether they are about to be attained or have already been attained.
These refer, respectively, to the objects of desire in the future, the present, and the past.
Third, there are four parts to the explanation of the scriptural passage concerning the six elements of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*).
First, citing scriptural evidence to provide an explanation;
second, clarifying the specific characteristics of the remedies;
third, resolving objections and difficulties.
The fourth [section] explains the distinctions between the five and six elements.
Therefore, the fact that loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] are not the direct antidotes to hatred, harm, and so forth,
demonstrates that when first practicing, one still gives rise to the conceit of "I" and has not yet eliminated doubt.
In order to subdue and cause the abandonment of all false attachments, this realm is established.
Within the specific modes of treatment, there are two parts;
first, the treatment categorized according to three types.
Regarding the subsequent treatment of the six lines individually:
the sixth [line] is established because it observes the ultimate correct principle (*yukti*).
That which is called the "correct principle" consists merely of the emptiness of the self (*ātman*) as clung to within the reality of cause and effect (*hetu-phala-tattva*).
By observing this, pride and doubt are extinguished.
[These are: first, malice; second, harmfulness; third, envy; fourth, delusion; and fifth, greed and anger.
This is explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
These correspond, in order, to the four types of remedies: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Here, it is stated that sympathetic joy remedies dissatisfaction, which is precisely envy (*īrṣyā*);
equanimity remedies both attachment (*lobha*) and aversion (*dveṣa*).
Ignorance is not mentioned because its objects of affection and aversion are not equal;
[the practitioner] gives rise to the practice of equanimity toward both within this context.
It speaks only of the remedies for the two [extremes].
The middle object, which accords with equanimity (*upekṣā*), is omitted and not mentioned;
yet in reality, it also excludes delusion (*moha*).
Regarding the phrase "if one is free from the conceit of self (asmimāna) in relation to one's own liberation," etc.:
not grasping at the conceit of self and being free from the fetters of grasping at conceit is called "liberation."
One will then be free from doubt regarding the truths realized, such as reality itself.
To resolve potential objections, it is said:
"These renunciations are certainly able to bring about renunciation from all forms of ill-will and the like."
That is to say, there is an objection:
"The cultivation of the six concentrations, such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), abandons the six types of opposites (*vipakṣa*), such as ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
Why, then, was it previously stated that loving-kindness and the others are not the direct antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to ill-will, harmfulness, and so forth?"
Now, this is explained as follows:
these various practices of renunciation, when brought to the stage of fulfillment, are certainly able to transcend all forms of ill-will and the like;
however, this is because they were not properly cultivated during the preceding stage of preparatory application.
Faults such as malice may still manifest;
therefore, the aforementioned [levels] are not the direct antidotes.
Regarding the statement that "the first four types are subsumed under the celestial abodes" (devasthāna), etc.:
Master Jing’s commentary explains:

Regarding the judgment here that the preceding gates of impurity-contemplation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*)— as superior to the marks of physical form (*rūpa-nimitta*)— are the "abodes of devas" (*deva-vihāra*),
they are designated as "abodes of devas" from the perspective of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) upon which they rely.
Because they are not exclusively the four immeasurables, they are not termed "Brahma-abodes.
As for why the four immeasurables are described as Brahma-abodes within these six gates,
it is based on their ability to induce Brahma-merit that they are so designated.
This is solely because it fully explains the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). Ji says:
"The two types, compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which are practiced based on the dhyānas, are called 'abodes of the gods' (*devavihāra*)."
The cultivation based on the immeasurables is called the Brahma-abodes.
Regarding the fourth [section], the explanation of being free from all faults as the basis for renunciation has three parts.
First, it indicates that there are four kinds of bases for renunciation.
Second, the detailed explanation of the reasons for the modes of practice;
third, the summary of the gains and losses regarding the four types and four periods.
The second section contains two parts.
First, the four persons are established separately as the basis for the cause;
subsequently, their modes of practice are explained in detail.
Regarding the statement that "because of their deceitful and fraudulent preaching, this is based on [the teaching] and not on a person (*pudgala*)," etc.:
There are those who, being deceitful and fraudulent, consider the teacher to be superior;
seeing his appearance and deportment, they then follow and learn from him.
Now, we cause them to rely on the Dharma and not on the person.
One must distinguish and resolve these matters through debate with others, realizing them for oneself rather than attaining realization merely by being close to a person;
furthermore, within this very context, there are further distinctions.
To further explain the aforementioned basis:
the Buddha, in accordance with worldly convention, employs two kinds of discourse—first, persons; second, dharmas.
Now, it is ordained that one should rely on the Dharma and not on the person.
One must not, upon hearing the Buddha’s words, follow them merely because they were spoken by a person;
for the Buddha conformed to worldly conventions of speech and should not be grasped as such.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of Dharma; this explains the second basis.
Because it accords with the world, it employs written words to express principles and meanings.
One should not consider merely hearing words that accord with the world to be the ultimate goal.

Therefore, it is said that one should rely on the meaning. Regarding the statement that "the sūtras spoken by the Buddha are either of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and so forth," this explains the third reliance.
Although one is instructed to rely on the meaning, one must not follow one's own views and grasp them as superior;
therefore, one relies on the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The fourfold characteristics of definitive meaning are as described elsewhere.
When the World-Honored One occasionally proclaims the reliances and so forth,
this explains the fourth reliance:
consciousness is taught as the cause for humans and devas.
Nirvana is explained through wisdom (*jñāna*).
In the definitive sutras (*nītārtha-sūtra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) is taught for those who have newly begun their practice,
while wisdom is taught for those who have practiced for a long time.
There are those who, upon hearing of the initial cultivation, immediately grasp it as the ultimate.
To preclude this, it is now said that one must rely on wisdom in order to attain the final goal.
Regarding the third bond,
the phrase "briefly based on whether there is loss or non-loss at four times" means that at the time of attaining the Dharma,
one relies on the wisdom that accords with the Dharma (*dharmajñāna*) and does not rely on the person.
When upholding the meaning, it is because one upholds the dharani of the non-literal meaning rather than the literal meaning;
when examining the meaning, it is because the wisdom that arises from resolving doubts relies upon the definitive meaning rather than the non-definitive meaning.
Regarding "the time of practicing in accordance with the Dharma":
"Dharma" refers to the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*); "practicing in accordance with the Dharma" refers to the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
When cultivating the path of renunciation, one relies on wisdom (*jñāna*), not consciousness (*vijñāna*).
These four reliances proceed from the initial stage to the subsequent stages;
they follow this sequence from the cultivation of the coarse to the cultivation of the subtle until final perfection is attained.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "it should be known that the establishment [of these] has already been explained," the preceding verse’s fivefold gate says:
"The distinctions between the general indication and the establishment of the characteristics of attention."
Having already explained the general headings and their systematic arrangement within the final miscellaneous topics that summarize the essential points of all the sūtras,
the third section below provides a combined explanation of the two gates of mental attention (*manasikāra*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
In this context, the object of focus is itself the sign (*nimitta*); thus,
the text is condensed into three parts,
the first of which is the introductory statement.
Next is the specific explanation;
later comes the general discussion.
Regarding the distinctions of *manasikāra* (attention), the following provides the specific explanation.
In the first part, the attention (*manasikāra*) is explained;
in the latter part, the object of focus (*ālambana*) is explained.
Within the former, there are three sections.
First, the names of the seven mental engagements (*manasikāra*) and the forty mental engagements are listed;
second, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the forty mental engagements are explained individually;
and finally, the inclusion of the seven mental engagements within the forty mental engagements is demonstrated.
The essence of attention (*manasikāra*) is the universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika-dharma*),
because its function increases when cultivating concentration and wisdom;
thus says the Abhidharma.
Regarding the increase of benefit through mental attention (*manasikāra*):
this refers to its being well-concordant with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
However, the explanation of the seven types of mental attention is given solely in terms of the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*).
The forty modes of mental attention (manasikāra) apply universally to both the states of meditative concentration and non-concentration; yet, although they apply to both,
they are for the most part cultivated based upon those specific stages.
Therefore, they are explained within the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
The characteristics of the seven modes of mental attention (*manasikāra*) will be explained extensively below in the forty-third fascicle, third section;
furthermore, they are subsumed under the four types of remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
The same applies to the ninth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*.

In the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth [chapters], it is explained how the seven types of attention (*manasikāra*) and the four types of attention are subsumed within the three kinds of yoga, and so forth;
all of this is as detailed therein.
Now, I shall briefly distinguish seven gates.
First is the gate of the three types of wisdom.
Master Jing’s commentary states:
The [first] three comprehensions correspond to all three types of wisdom (*prajñā*);
the latter six correspond only to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*). Master Ji says:
The single type of "comprehending characteristics" (lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī) penetrates both wisdom derived from hearing and wisdom derived from cultivation;
the remaining six are exclusively wisdom derived from cultivation, or alternatively, all seven are wisdom derived from cultivation.
The second [type of object] consists of names and meanings as conditions; the consciousnesses that apprehend characteristics take both names and meanings as their conditions,
while the remaining six take only meaning as their condition.
Regarding the three outflows (āsrava) and the outflow-free (anāsrava),
the eightieth [treatise] states that they all pertain to the outflowing (sāsrava).
Regarding the four gates of the three trainings:
the mental application (*manasikāra*) that realizes the characteristics, practices, culmination, and fruit pertains to all three trainings.

The remaining five types of mental application—those of the learners (*śaikṣa*), those of the non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), and those that pertain to neither—do not pertain to the training of the non-learner.
As in the "Compendium of Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*),
regarding the five gates of the four paths,
Master Ki (Kuiji) explains as follows:
The attention of observation regarding the resolution of characteristics pertains to both the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*);
the attention of detachment pertains solely to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*);
and the attention of delight in withdrawal pertains to all four paths.
The preparatory ultimate mental application (*prayoga-niṣṭha-manasikāra*) pertains to both the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*);
the seventh mental application pertains solely to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
These are cultivated by those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) based upon these four paths.
In the subsequent stages, all preparatory practices (*prayoga*) and clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) constitute the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) for the preceding stage;
this is not the case for a bodhisattva,
because it is possible for them to possess all four paths in each and every moment.
The underlying principle should be understood accordingly.
Now, based on the separation from the various stages (*bhūmi*),
because of the superior resolve that realizes the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-prativedha-adhimokṣa*), it universally leads to the superior progress and induces the immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
The mental attention of observation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*) also extends to the stage of application (*prayoga*).
Since the subsequent category is the superior progress (*viśeṣa-gamana*) of the preceding category,
it is said that the sixth [mental attention] also extends to superior progress.
The general basis consists of the nine stages, and the actual meaning is thus established through the seven gates of mental attention (*manasikāra*).

Regarding the sixty-two [types of practitioners]: those included in the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) characterized by the resolution of signs (*lakṣaṇa-pratibimba-adhimokṣa*) consist of the mental attentions of "separation" (*viveka*) and "culmination of application" (*prayoga-niṣṭha*); those included in the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) consist of the mental attention of "delight" (*rati*); those included in the fourfold path consist of the mental attention of "examination" (*mīmāṃsā*); and those included in the path of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*) consist of the same.
This is explained in reference to the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) for the specific separation from the higher defilements following the initial departure from the defilements of desire.
It is stated thus because there is room for further progress;
it does not mean that a subsequent path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is itself the preceding path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
The *prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra* (the attention of the culmination of preparation) occurs only immediately [before the path of seeing].

The *mīmāṃsā-manasikāra* (the attention of investigation) is said, based on the abandonment of the medium-grade [defilements] during the path of cultivation, to pertain only to the path of special progress (*viśeṣamārga*);
it is not stated that what follows constitutes the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
Nor is there any contradiction.
The meaning of the seventh mental application (*manasikāra*) as the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) can be understood by analogy;
therefore, it is not mentioned in the treatise.
Sixth, the three types of yoga practitioners are subsumed [as follows].
Master Ki says:
First, there are two kinds of beginners.
First, regarding the practitioner who is a beginner in the cultivation of attention (*manasikāra*):
they dwell upon a single object and diligently cultivate attention until they have attained the cultivated attention and are still unable to realize one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*).
Second, regarding the beginner who seeks purification from afflictions:
this refers to one who has already attained the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that is to be cultivated,
and who, desiring to purify the mind from all afflictions, correctly and diligently practices the mental attention of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisamvedī manasikāra*).
Second, the yoga practitioner who has already practiced is one who has well cultivated the five intermediate mental orientations (*manasikāra*).
