Third, the yoga practitioner who has transcended mental orientation.

This refers to abiding in the seventh stage of mental attention (*manasikāra*), having transcended the cultivation of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and attained the fruit of that cultivation.
According to this, these three types of practitioners—
along with twenty-eight others— are said to be those who have "begun their practice" (*ādikarmika*) regarding the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
The aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are termed "already practiced" (*abhyasta-caryā*).
Following the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), they are termed "transcending mental attention" (*atikrānta-manasikāra*);
that is, the aspect of clear manifestation (*vibhūta-nimitta*) exists within the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

If one were to say that the intention of the next five [applications of mindfulness] lies in the stage of "conducive to penetration" (nirvedhabhāgīya), and that the intention of the seventh lies after the "clear realization of the truths" (satyābhisamaya).
This would contradict the passage concerning the inclusion of the three characteristics— such as being "in training" (śaikṣa) and so forth— within the forty modes of attention (*manasikāra*).
For all seven types of attention pertain to those in training,
while the first and the seventh also pertain to those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

From this, it is known that the three types of yoga practitioners have distinct assignments according to their respective stages, and thus their correlation with the seven mental attentions (*manasikāra*) differs.
These two systems are inherently distinct;
one must not conflate the three types of yoga practitioners with the sevenfold correlation.
This clearly demonstrates that the three stages of the seven mental attentions (*manasikāra*) are likewise so;
one should not give rise to further conceptual proliferation regarding this.
Nevertheless, the twenty-eight types of practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*) are collectively assigned to the seven mental attentions.
The seven mental attentions (manasikāra) are not assigned to three specific stages;
for instance, the seven mental attentions are present in those who are neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
and they are also present on the path of accumulation (sambhāramārga) within the stage of a learner (śaikṣa).
Because one first proceeds to abandon defilements by means of the mundane path,
there is also a path of equipment (sambhāramārga) in which the seven mental orientations (manaskāra) are not cultivated and meditative concentration is not cultivated;
it is only within the path of application (prayogamārga) that the seven mental orientations are fully perfected as one proceeds to abandon the nine grades of defilement of the desire realm.

After attaining clear observation (*abhisamaya*), one also gives rise to the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) in order to progress toward detachment from the defilements of the higher stages.

Regarding the seven [mental attentions] in terms of the gate of the conventional and the real: the three—namely, the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*), the attention of resolute belief (*ādhimokṣika*), and the attention of the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*)—pervade both the conventional and the real.

The following clarifies that these three [types of attention] subsume both the attention consisting of resolute belief (*adhimokṣika-manasikāra*) and the attention consisting of reality (*tattvārtha-manasikāra*);
whereas the attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*) subsumes only the attention consisting of resolute belief, and thus takes only the conventional (*prajñapti*) as its object.
The remaining three modes of attention exclusively take reality as their object,
because the uninterrupted path takes only suchness as its object; this is according to the previous classification.
The remaining categories should be applied accordingly, as will be explained below.
These forty types of mental attention constitute eleven classes.
First, the meanings of the first two teachings;
second, the four foundations of mindfulness;
third, the two categories of the conventional and the real.
Fourth, the three categories of ordinary beings and noble ones;
fifth, the three categories of abandonment—initial, middle, and final;
sixth, the four types of objects of focus.
7. Six categories of cultivation and realization free from defilement;
8. Four paths; 9. Four stages of cultivation.
The fourteen categories of wisdom-concentration attain mastery by being free from hindrances.
Among the eleven, four, and three categories of mental attention pertaining to the causes and fruits of the three vehicles,
the first four categories serve as the common cause for all.
The latter seven categories serve as the distinguishing causes solely for those in the stages of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding the detailed explanation of the forty [categories],
"conditioning by phenomena" refers to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) taking meanings as its object.
Those who practice through reflection and cultivation are said to rely on the predominant [object], not merely on the object itself;
for even the cultivation that takes meaning as its condition through hearing and so forth also takes the teaching as its object. As for the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*):
Regarding the *Abhidharma* (Dharmapada), the eleventh [chapter] states: "Mental attention that is exclusively mundane" refers to true mental attention (*bhūta-manasikāra*).
The *Abhidharma* further states: "Mental attention that is exclusively supramundane and that which is subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*)."

These are fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). What is referred to here as "contemplating all phenomena through their specific and general characteristics" is precisely subsequently attained wisdom.
The principle of true suchness (*tathatā*) is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
There are two types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) for those in training (*śaikṣa*):
first, that which is intrinsic, whose nature is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the second point, concerning those that exist within the continuum, they are distinguished by way of the body.

Within the body of one in training (*śaikṣa*), all wholesome mental attentions (*manasikāra*), whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), are called "mental attentions of one in training.
As for "the mental attention of thorough knowledge" and so forth:
Jingyun: There may be those who, through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), subsequently attain a mind that takes external objects as its focus, such as names (*nāman*).
Because this is not a correct realization (*samyag-abhisamaya*), it cannot eradicate the afflictions (*kleśa*).
There may be those who fully comprehend suffering but, because they do not contemplate suchness (*tathatā*), are unable to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Those whose mental attention (*manasikāra*) is correctly directed toward severance perform both tasks simultaneously:
they fully comprehend suchness and are further able to sever the afflictions.
Master Ji says:
"The mental application of universal knowledge (*parijñā-manasikāra*) is the remote path of preparation (*dūramārga*);
the mental application of correct abandonment (*samyakprahāṇa-manasikāra*) is the proximate path of preparation (*āsannamārga*) and the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*)."
"Attention that has already abandoned [the object]" refers to the remaining two paths.
Regarding "attention to conceptual and non-conceptual images," the essence and objects of conceptualization are the minds and mental factors of the three realms.
The conceptualization of names subsumes all phenomena of the three realms.
Among the five dharmas, it is the conceptualization of the "name" within the category of "characteristics.
These two function as the objective sphere, and their essential substance is one.
They are divided into two types because of the distinction between *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
The eleventh chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"There is the conceptualized image (*savikalpa-pratibimba*)."
The object of focus for concentration and wisdom when employing attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) is the non-conceptual image (*nirvikalpa-pratibimba*).
The object of focus for concentration and wisdom when employing attention to reality (*tattva-manasikāra*) is the [actual] object itself.
The śamatha and vipaśyanā based on that tainted (sāsrava) mental attention are called "conceptual images," because their essence is false conceptualization (abhūtaparikalpa).
Tainted-free (anāsrava) śamatha and vipaśyanā are called "non-conceptual images."
Because its essence is not false or deceptive. Herein,
the essence of discrimination is designated by way of the object of focus (*ālambana*),
while the subjective factors of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are divided into two kinds.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Regarding "the accomplishment of what is to be done at the limit of phenomena," Master Jing says:
Judging by the subsequent text,
the first two stages are prior to the path of seeing (bhūmipūrva),
while these latter two belong to the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning (darśana-bhāvanā-aśaikṣa).
Non-conceptual wisdom takes that suchness as its object; this very essence of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena pervades all names and things, reaching their ultimate limit.
Regarding the accomplishment of what is to be done, among the objects of focus and mental attention, it is first explained in terms of the cause.
Because within the causal stage as well, there exists the principle of accomplishing and realizing [the goal] according to one's respective capacity.

That is to say, "I contemplate in such and such a manner" means that, based on the causes, one personally severs suffering and its origin; it is not merely a single instance of saying "in such a manner."
If I contemplate in such and such a manner,
I instead take as my object the causes for cultivating and realizing cessation and the path;
since cessation and the path are not singular, I speak of them repeatedly as "such and such."
"There may be such and such [beings]. Furthermore, he causes sentient beings to realize that there "may be such and such" abandonment of the origin of suffering;
he repeats "such and such" because the origin of suffering is not singular.
Thus one cultivates and realizes cessation and the path.
Since cessation and the path are not singular, it is said "thus" repeatedly.
Next, because one takes the fruit as an object, it is said: "and taking as an object the pure object of focus through mental attention."
Regarding the lower [level] of mutual inclusion: within the context of those causes,
the tasks previously performed take the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) as their initial gateway,
while taking the fruit of Buddhahood as their final gateway.
It encompasses only the *manasikāra* that is the fruit of the culmination of application;
during its stage of cultivation, there is no further distinct object,
as it reaches back toward the three aforementioned types of objects.
Regarding "the attention that accomplishes what is to be done" (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānālambanamanasikāra*), it refers to such thoughts as "I contemplate thus.
Based on the subsequent text, this is determined to pertain exclusively to the state of Buddhahood, which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
However, in this present passage, the attention is first distinguished according to self-benefit and benefit for others within the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).
This is explained subsequently in relation to the fruition. As for the statement,

"I contemplate such and such," because it is the principle of the causal conditions for śamatha and vipaśyanā within the path of insight (darśanamārga) that is free from signs, it is collectively termed the "object-limit of phenomena" (*vastuparyantatālambana*).
Within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), there are no further distinct objects;
it remotely takes the three preceding objects as its focus.

Furthermore, if these three preceding objects exist within the Buddha-stage (*buddha-bhūmi*), they are collectively termed the "attention focused on the accomplishment of what was to be done" (*kṛtaniṣṭhita-kṛtya-manasikāra*).
Master Ji’s commentary on the "accomplishment of the limits of phenomena" contradicts the *Abhidharma-śāstra* and the following twenty-six [verses];
these shall be explained when we reach them.
Regarding the mental application that takes as its object the accomplishment of what is to be done at the limit of the subject matter,
there are two interpretations.
One interpretation is the same as that in the Abhidharma.
This means that the first is the nature of the extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).
The nature of the extent of existence refers to the fact that the entities and phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are only as many as they are.

The nature of the mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) refers to the four noble truths, the sixteen aspects, suchness, the impermanence of all conditioned things, the suffering of all conditioned things, the selflessness of all phenomena, the tranquility of nirvana, emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness.
This is solely the principle of the truths (*satya*).
Whether by way of the doors of the truths, the doors of practice (*caryā*), the doors of the summaries of all phenomena (*dharmoddāna*), or the doors of liberation,
that which realizes the principles of the aforementioned aggregates, bases, and elements through their distinctions of meaning is called "the nature of things as they are" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
The essence of the accomplishment of what is to be done is itself the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*);
this reveals the first essence.
The nature of the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) pertains solely to subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
The nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) pertains to both fundamental and subsequent knowledge.
The accomplishment of what is to be done refers to the two types of transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*): namely, *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.

Within this context, the objects of focus regarding the limits of phenomena—the body, sensation, mind, and dharmas—constitute both the nature of things as they are in their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
The accomplishment of what was to be done is precisely the two-fold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
That is to say, when I contemplate "this and that," this is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) taking the self-nature of phenomena as its object;
when I contemplate "such and such," this is the subsequently attained wisdom taking the specific distinctions of phenomena as its object.
"That it is thus and thus" refers to the realization of the self-nature by means of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
"That it is to be distinguished as such and such" refers to the realization of specific distinctions by means of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Although the nature of true thusness (tathatā) is not differentiated by phenomena,
correct cognition (samyagjñāna) accords with and realizes it through the practice of differentiated activities based on preparatory application (prayoga).
It is also described as twofold:
when one contemplates in such and such a manner, it is the cause of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*);
if one contemplates in this or that way, it is the cause of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
When there is such and such, this is the fruit of subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*);
one should distinguish such and such as the fruit of fundamental knowledge (*mūla-jñāna*).
This above provides a general exposition of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of enlightenment.
The pure object of focus is nirvāṇa, which is the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*).
Although this interpretation accords with the Abhidharma,
it does not accord with the inclusion [of the objects] within the seven types mentioned below.
The second explanation states:
This differs from what is taught in the Abhidharma.
"The limit of phenomena" (*vastuparyanta*) refers to the ultimate limit of the objects—namely, the body, sensation, mind, and dharmas—which serve as conditions in the present.
"Accomplishing what is to be done" refers to the principles for accomplishing present tasks and future objectives.
Regarding this, there are three interpretations.
The first says:
I reflect that such-and-such is the object of a distracted mind,
whereas such-and-such is the object of a concentrated mind; by performing this reflection on the distracted mind, [one attains stability].
Because one has formed this settled thought that "in the end,
there shall be such and such a definitive result," there will ultimately be the definitive realization of that decisive result.
The second [type] says:
"To contemplate 'it is thus and thus' is the causal condition for the essential characteristic (*bhāva-nimitta*);
by virtue of this contemplation, there will arise the fruit of definitive resolution (niścaya) that it is indeed thus and thus."
If I contemplate such and such a thing, it is a sign consisting of a mental image;
by virtue of this contemplation, I shall achieve the result of decisive resolution in such and such a manner.
Third, it is said:
"I contemplate that such-and-such is the self-nature of dependent phenomena;
by virtue of this contemplation, there shall arise such-and-such a definitive result."
If I contemplate such and such a thing, this is the meaning of the differentiation of dharmas as conditions;
by virtue of this contemplation, one shall discern such and such a result of definitive resolution.
This above section generally clarifies the accomplishment of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Although it contradicts the Abhidharma, it accords with the textual structure of the subsequent section on the seven aspects of inclusion.
Furthermore, regarding "the attention that takes pure objects as its focal point":
There are two explanations for this.
One says: it is the mental attention that takes true suchness as its object.
The second says:
Because one takes this untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*) as the object of focus, it is called "mental attention that takes a pure object of focus."
The attention of discernment that surpasses external [objects] refers to one who initially discerns all phenomena;
this is the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*). It is preceded by *śamatha*.

Based on the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) and analytical discernment (*pravicaya*), one engages in the mental attention of tranquility (*śamatha-manasikāra*). This refers to the initial placement of the mind within;
at this stage of wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), one stabilizes the mind through meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Vipaśyanā as the foremost" refers to the meditative equipoise cultivated during the stage of wisdom through cultivation;
by means of the mental application of resolute conviction and analytical investigation, one purifies knowledge and vision.
"Because wisdom is the means for fulfilling wisdom.
Regarding "tranquility arises through the mental application of tranquility":
concentration is the means, because concentration is brought to fulfillment.

Because of practicing the mental application of partial and complete cultivation, one attains liberation of the mind from the hindrances; because of practicing the mental application with uninterrupted and earnest attention, one attains liberation from the fetters.
The five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) and nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*) actually encompass both the manifest and the seed states;
however, they are specifically designated as "hindrances" here because their manifest activity is predominant.
This is because seeds are difficult to sever, as their characteristics are submerged and subtle.
Now, these are specifically taught as fetters;
therefore, they are said to be abandoned separately.

Regarding the mental attention of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*): it refers to that by which one correctly abandons all afflictions (*kleśa*), maintains their abandonment, and causes the afflictions to remain distant from the continuum.

Master Jing’s commentary explains that when the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) arises in the present, it realizes analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and is thus termed "sustaining" (*pratigraha*) the abandonment;
it does not mean that the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arising is what is called sustaining.

Master Ji’s commentary explains that the mental application of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*) subsumes the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),

as well as the two paths of further progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*)— namely, those conducive to purification (*vyavadāna-anukūla*) and those conducive to investigation (*pratyavekṣā-anukūla*)— both near and far.
Alternatively, pure wisdom may not be subsumed under the four paths.
The six recollections refer to the recollection of the Buddha and so forth, as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Spontaneous mental engagement refers to the four occasions, the first of which is the occasion of attaining mental engagement.
Regarding the lower [stages], when one attains the sixth and seventh mental states through mutual inclusion, there are two moments:
the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) which abandons the ninth grade of defilement, and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
This refers to the time when one correctly enters and has already entered the fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*).
By attaining these two types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), one is able to correctly enter the foundational dhyānas (*mūladhyāna*).
These two preceding stages constitute the preliminary application (*prayoga*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

At the time of the threefold cultivation of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), through this preliminary application, one enters the path of seeing and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) to cultivate clear realization.

Regarding the fourth period, the stage of arhatship: "attaining" refers to the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), while "having attained" refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Within the inclusion of the third seven types of mental attention and the forty aspects:
First, the characteristics of the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) are clarified.
However, their mutual inclusion will be analyzed according to the text.

The mental attention that comprehends characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manasikāra*) is able to comprehend the coarse characteristics of the lower stages and the tranquil characteristics of the higher stages.
In this initial stage of mental application (*manasikāra*), hearing and reflection are still intermingled.
From this point onward, one is exclusively engaged with the signs of cultivation;
one repeatedly contemplates these signs of coarseness and tranquility, repeatedly giving rise to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
This is called the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*). Through the cultivation of this,
the path of initial abandonment arises, along with its corresponding attention.
Because it is called the mental attention of "separation," all superior-grade afflictions and coarse heavinesses have been completely severed; furthermore,
one takes joy in further superior abandonment.
Having seen the merit of the aforementioned abandonment,
one touches upon a slight degree of the joy and bliss of seclusion;
furthermore, in order to eliminate lethargy and drowsiness, one repeatedly cultivates calm and sublime mental attention.
Because it gladdens the mind,
it is called the attention of "delighting in cultivation.
Thus, by means of this, the practitioner is sustained by the requisites for the category of wholesome qualities.
This causes the afflictions, entanglements, and stains associated with the desire realm that are comprised within the medium grade to no longer manifest.
For this reason, one examines whether the afflictions have been abandoned or not.
Again, by further applying the mind to observation,
there arises a conforming sign of tranquility;
this is called the attention of observation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*).
In this way, the practitioner repeatedly observes and cultivates the remedies in order to achieve temporary dissociation from all afflictions of the desire realm.
Because this attention associated with the path of counteraction is the final preparatory application (*prayoga-paryavasāna-manasikāra*) of the first dhyāna,
it is called the "preparatory application that has reached its culmination.
By means of this, all minor afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm cease to function.
Immediately following this, one realizes the fundamental first dhyāna together with its concomitant mental attention (*manaskāra*);
this is called the mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala-manaskāra*).
Among these, it is difficult for the path that abandons the superior grade of afflictions to arise at the very beginning.
Therefore, two types of attention (*manasikāra*) serve as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Since it is difficult to sever even the final, inferior grade of the lower stages, let alone the initial cultivation,
one type of attention serves as the preparatory application.
Immediately following the preceding category, there can be the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) of the subsequent category;
therefore, for the middle three categories of abandonment, the preparatory path is not mentioned.
Immediately following the subsequent category, there can be the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the preceding category.
It is not said that there is a path of liberation for the abandonment of the first six [categories of afflictions],
because one enters the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) upon completing the abandonment of the final three categories; therefore,
the seventh mental application (*manaskāra*) is designated as the path of liberation.
Having clarified the characteristics of the seven types of mental attention,
one should now analyze them according to the text.
Regarding the "comprehension of the characteristics" which encompasses the apprehension of phenomena and their meanings:
Master Ji said:
"There are two interpretations of this. One says:"
Because the wisdom that comprehends characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pratisaṃvedī*) involves both hearing and cultivation, it subsumes two types [of wisdom].
One school asserts that the wisdom that comprehends characteristics is exclusively the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).
This explains that because the initial arising of cultivation also takes the Dharma as its object, it is said to encompass both [types of wisdom].

What was previously described as taking the Dharma as its object refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); what is described here pertains to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
It is not contradictory that what is narrow in the front is broad in the rear.
Now, based on this passage, we shall distinguish whether the three types of wisdom are deficient or complete within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
One interpretation holds that the realm of form also possesses the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), in agreement with the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
He said: "The three types of wisdom exist in the realms of desire and form; like the householder Hatthaka, one is born in the Atapa Heaven and teaches the Dharma there.
If a person teaches the Dharma, they must contemplate its meaning."
Therefore, one should know that the realm of form (rūpadhātu) also possesses wisdom derived from reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā),
whereas in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) there is only wisdom derived from cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā). Thus, this text says:
The *manaskāra* of "comprehending characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) encompasses the meaning of the object.

As for what was previously called the "manaskāra of the object-meaning," this refers to the manaskāra associated with the wisdoms produced by reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Since it does not say that it encompasses only one part of the meaning of the object, but rather says it encompasses the meaning of the object as a whole, [it is understood as such].

Therefore, one should know that the "characteristic-discerning" (*lakṣaṇapraveśa*) attention is associated with both wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Furthermore, since the treatise states that this characteristic-discerning stage is still interspersed with hearing and reflection, yet it refers to it as "attention belonging to the dhyāna stages" (*dhyānabhūmika-manasikāra*).
Thus we know that the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) also possesses wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Jing’s statement that "the characteristic of penetration (*tiao-xiang*) applies to all three types of wisdom" likely refers to this.

Furthermore, the ninth fascicle of the *Abhidharma* states that one generates the correct means for the sake of the object sought through the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*).
The Master [Paramārtha] explains this as follows:
This is a further explanation of the mental application of resolute belief (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*).
"The object sought" refers to the object to be abandoned below and the object to be attained above.
Regarding the statement "giving rise to the correct application":
this refers to the application for cultivating wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) in order to sever the afflictions;
it consists of all mental attentions (*manasikāra*) associated with hearing and reflection that differ from those previously mentioned.
The former is not mixed with hearing and reflection;
this [latter] takes only that which is associated with hearing and reflection.
This is the intended meaning of the commentary.

The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) also possesses wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). There is another interpretation which holds that the realm of form possesses only wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī*) and wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*), but lacks wisdom derived from reflection;
this is the same as the Sarvāstivāda position.
However, as for this text stating that "the meaning of 'comprehending the characteristics' encompasses the meaning of 'conditioning'":
the scope of the meaning of conditioning is broad.

If one is in the desire realm, the mental application (manasikāra) that constitutes the meaning of conditioning occurs together with volition (cetanā) and wisdom derived from reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā).
Those in the upper realms possess both [the wisdom of hearing and] the wisdom of cultivation;

therefore, the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) includes both the objects of phenomena (*dharmālambana*) and the objects of meaning (*arthālambana*) belonging to the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*),
but does not include those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Since the text has already established the seven types of attention by way of the stages—
ranging from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
why is it necessary to separately distinguish those that take the phenomena of the desire realm as their object and those that take the meaning of those phenomena as their object?
Therefore, it is not said that they "encompass a portion" and so forth;
rather, it is stated that "discerning characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisamvedī*) is a mixture of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*),
because this [stage] is interspersed with the hearing and reflection belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because the *anāgamya* concentration is proximate to the desire realm, it alternates between emerging from and entering [meditative absorption], and thus is mixed with hearing (*śruta*).
From this stage upward, one transcends hearing and reflection, as the characteristics are exclusively those of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Master Ji and others explain the gateway of the three types of wisdom as follows:

the wisdom that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) consists of both hearing and cultivation; the remaining six consist only of cultivation, or alternatively, all seven consist of cultivation.
The meaning of this can be understood.

Regarding the statement that "the three— the comprehension of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapraveśa*), resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), and the ultimate fruit (*niṣṭhāphala*)— comprehensively include the attention of reality through resolute conviction (*tattvārthādhimokṣamanasikāra*) and so forth," Jing says:
From this text, it is known that the mental application of resolute belief (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) encompasses both provisional and ultimate contemplations,
whereas the mental application of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*) includes only the forty types of resolute belief among them.
Among the seven [types of attention], the remaining three types of attention encompass only the "true reality" among the forty;
this is according to the former method. As for the other method, it should be understood that they apply as appropriate.
Among the forty types of attention, the seventh clarifies the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*).

This refers to the practitioner of dhyāna who, according to their desire, takes the mental application of superimposition (*adhyāropamanasikāra*) upon various objective signs as the preliminary gateway.
Next, the nineteenth [mental application] is called the mental application of discerning through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣavikalpamanasikāra*).
That is to say, by means of this, there may first be the discernment of phenomena;
this is either the wisdom of reflection belonging to the desire realm or śamatha as the primary factor.
This constitutes the subsequent gateway.
If, according to the former method, attention through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) is merely a conceptual visualization,
it is therefore subsumed only under the seventh [type], attention consisting of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*).
If, however, it is according to the latter method, attention through resolute conviction may or may not be subsumed within the seven types of attention.

That is to say, there may be cases where either the initial investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) or calm abiding (*śamatha*) serves as the primary factor for all seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*); therefore,
it is said that regarding the latter category, one should understand that they apply accordingly.
Master Ji’s commentary explains:
"The three—the result of the culmination of the resolution that realizes characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-adhimokṣa*)—comprehensively include the attention of true reality (*tattvamanasikāra*).
This is because the realization of characteristics is present both during the initial stage of cultivation and in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
In the beginning, all cultivation consists solely of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*);
for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and others, cultivation is mostly based on reality (*bhūtārtha*).
Since resolute conviction serves as the immediate preparatory application (*prayoga*), its principle applies to both the provisional and the real.
Regarding the statement that the "attention to the ultimate fruit" (*niṣṭhā-phala-manasikāra*) is present at all times and stages within the fundamental stage (*mūlabhūmi*),
and that the "attention to observation" (*paryeṣaṇā-manasikāra*) comprises only the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*):
this is because the latter consists of the three grades of the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*).
Initially, when cultivating through provisional understanding, one does not speak of penetrating the reality;
however, for the subsequent preparatory application (*prayoga*), the principle also extends to the ultimate truth.
As for the other three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), they pertain exclusively to the ultimate reality.
"Because the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) frequently contemplates the truth":
this refers to the preceding section. "As for the remaining sections, it should be understood that they correspond accordingly":
this refers to how the seven types of mental engagement (*manasikāra*) previously explained are subsumed within the two [categories].

Regarding other specific meanings: the "ascertainment of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapraveśamanasikāra*) is predominantly characterized by resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), because it is the initial arising of cultivation;
the "ultimate fruit" (*niṣṭhāphala*) consists solely of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) in its true reality (*bhūtārtha*);

and the "contemplative attention" (*mīmāṃsāmanasikāra*) pertains to both resolute conviction and true reality, as it can serve as the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) and the preparatory path (*prayogamārga*).
The remaining four are as previously described.
Therefore, it is said that one should understand the application according to the other gates as appropriate;
it is not stated that all seven types differ from those preceding them.
There is an explanation:
the preceding text explained the characteristics of correct mental attention (*tattvamanasikāra*),

namely, the mental attention that reflects upon all phenomena according to principle by way of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of suchness (*tathatālakṣaṇa*).
Now, this text takes that which has both specific and general characteristics as its primary category,
because it is taught as being common to the three vehicles;
it takes that which has suchness as its object as the remaining category.
It is because this applies specifically to Bodhisattvas.
If one approaches it from other perspectives, that which is not characterized by the marks of full realization (apariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa) is also considered the universal ultimate truth;
therefore, it is said to be "according to the circumstances."
Regarding the statement that the two types of mental attention also include the mental attention of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):
this is because, having attained the fruit, one repeatedly gives rise to a sense of weary detachment, and thus possesses the aspect of discernment (*sanimitta*).
Furthermore, regarding the abandonment of the afflictions, the five middle types of mental attention are taught based on the path.
Because those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) no longer possess them, they are not said to have them.
As for the "comprehensive knowledge through observation" (*parīkṣā-parijñā*), observation also extends to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
The observation that [this stage] comprises only those with conceptual discrimination is because wisdom arises predominantly during the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*);
it is for this reason that it is specifically so described, yet it is not without non-conceptual [wisdom].
Regarding the statement that "the mental application (manasikāra) of the object-limit (vastuparyanta) encompasses all [seven types of mental application]," Jing’s commentary explains:

among the seven mental applications, it includes those of "separation" (viveka), "delight in cultivation" (bhāvanābhirati), "culmination of application" (prayoganiṣṭha), and "fruit of culmination of application" (prayoganiṣṭhāphala).
Among these four, the first three are the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and definitely take suchness (*tathatā*) as their object.
The fruit of the culmination of the preparatory stage (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala*), which is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), also takes suchness as its object.
All of these are included within the mental application (*manasikāra*) that takes the limit of phenomena (*vastu-paryanta*) as its object.
The remaining [mental engagements] consist of the mental engagement of observation with the conviction of the characteristic of realization;
these either pertain to the path of means, being associated with the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) while seeking to realize suchness,

or they pertain to the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*), being associated with subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*) during the observation that reflexively takes as its object the suchness realized therein.
Although the aspect (ākāra) appears as if external to the mind, it may still be termed an "object that is the limit of the entity" (*vastuparyantālambana*).
Therefore, all seven types of mental attention (*manaskāra*) are subsumed under the mental attention that has the limit of the entity as its object.

Regarding the accomplishment of what is to be done: if one follows the first approach, all [mental attentions] are universally subsumed; if one follows the second approach, they are subsumed solely within the mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala-manaskāra*).
Regarding the aforementioned "attention that accomplishes what is to be done" (*kāryapariniṣpattālambanamanasikāra*),
it refers to thinking, "I shall contemplate in such and such a manner," and so forth.
This is the first gateway, which explains this attention that accomplishes what is to be done by way of its causes.
Therefore, it subsumes the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*). This is based on their sequential differentiation into seven;
subsequently, it mentions "and the mental attention that takes pure objects as its focal point."
Regarding this second section, since the accomplishment of the task is explained solely in terms of the result,
it is subsumed exclusively under the *manasikāra* of the "result of the culmination of application" (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala*). As Ki states:
Regarding the first gate, because it is accomplished based on the cultivation of conditioned fruits, it is subsumed under all seven [categories].

As for the second gate, that which is subsumed solely under the fruit of the culmination of application refers to the aforementioned second mental attention (*manasikāra*) regarding the purification of the object of focus, which exists only in the state of Buddhahood.

Because the ultimate transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not subsumed under either initial resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) or analytical attention (*pravicaya-manasikāra*); however, when śamatha is taken as the primary factor, it is universally subsumed within all [categories].

Regarding what was previously stated concerning the attention of resolute conviction and analytical investigation: some first analytically investigate all phenomena, while others take śamatha as their primary focus.
This initial attention of resolute conviction and analytical investigation is precisely the wisdom of excellent reflection born of desire.
It is not subsumed under the seven types of attention belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
However, if one relies on the *śamatha* within the form realm and performs that resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) and analytical investigation (*pravicaya*),
it is then subsumed under the seven types of attention.
The preceding text further mentions "mental attention to tranquility" (*śamatha-manasikāra*).
This refers to that by means of which one either initially settles the mind within or takes vipaśyanā as the primary focus.

Regarding the statement, "Now, it should be known that if there is initial tranquility (*śamatha*) or if insight (*vipaśyanā*) is the primary factor, it is likewise so," this refers to what was previously stated:
"Alternatively, one may initially settle the mind within."

If the attention of tranquility (*śamatha-manasikāra*) that abides in internal objects while initially relying on a mind belonging to the desire realm is not included within the seven types of attention;
however, if the attention of tranquility arises based on the insight (*vipaśyanā*) of cultivated wisdom, it is indeed included among the seven types of attention.
Regarding the statement that "the first six types of attention encompass both partial and complete cultivation," Ji says:
"There are those liberated through wisdom who cultivate wisdom but are not in meditative absorption— namely, ordinary beings."
Attaining the fundamental dhyāna does not necessarily entail the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the mental application (*manasikāra*) of the ultimate fruit, it is said— on the basis of the preeminent case— that it comprises the complete cultivation,
because for one liberated through both [tranquility and insight], the cultivation is complete.
Regarding the statement that "conforming attention (*ānulomika-manasikāra*) is included in the first two [stages]," etc.:
conforming attention is included in the first two because it involves the repudiation of the object of focus (*ālambana*).

Counteractive attention (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*) is included in the stage of "separation" (*viveka*), the "preparatory application" (*prayoga-niṣṭha*), and a portion of "delight in cultivation" (*ruci-saṃgraha*), because it constitutes the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Regarding the statement that "the attention of conforming to purification (*anuloma-viśuddhi-manasikāra*) is subsumed only by one portion of the attention of delight (*abhirati-manasikāra*)," Master Jing says:
Regarding the previous explanation of the attention that accords with purification (*viśuddhānulomamanasikāra*):
it refers to the cultivation of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) or the contemplation of any one sublime object (*praṇīta-vastu*) by means of which [purification occurs].
Within that attention of delighting in [the path] (*ratisaṃgrāhakamanasikāra*), all four paths are fully present.
The "attention to purity" (*śuddhā-manasikāra*) subsumes only one portion of the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

Furthermore, the principle of cultivating the six recollections (*anusmṛti*) and so forth should also be included within that "attention to investigation" (*paryeṣaka-manasikāra*), because they are likewise paths of superior progress and are easy to understand; therefore, they are not mentioned separately.
Furthermore, one may cultivate the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) or focus on any single sublime object; however, these do not sever the afflictions, as they are subsumed under the four paths.
They constitute only a portion of the *āsvādanā-manasikāra* (the attention of relishing).
Because it is not a path of further progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*),
it does not include the attention of investigation consisting of the resolution that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisamvedī adhimokṣamanasikāra*).
Therefore, one should know that the attention of joy in cultivation (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra*) encompasses both the four paths and that which is not the four paths.
Furthermore, it is explained:

the statement that "the attention of observing what has been abandoned and what has not yet been abandoned is subsumed under the attention of observation alone" refers to its inclusion within the antidote of abandonment; as for other cases, one should understand them according to their respective applications.
Regarding the previously explained "attention of conforming observation":
it refers to that by means of which one observes whether the various afflictions have been abandoned or not,
or alternatively, observes what one has realized for oneself and what was previously realized.
The mental application of contemplating the principles of all phenomena and so forth;
if one relies on contemplating whether the various afflictions have been abandoned or not yet abandoned,
this explains the mental application of conforming observation.

That is to say, it conforms to and encompasses only the "contemplative attention" (manasikāra) among the seven types, because these two are identical in employing the path of antidote for abandonment as their means. Therefore, it is said:
"This is explained from the perspective of the antidote for abandonment."

If one follows the sequence of the text, it further states: "Alternatively, one observes the principles of the various phenomena realized by oneself and previously examined," and so forth; this explains the *manasikāra* of conforming observation (*anulomika-manasikāra*).

The attention of sequential observation (*ānulomika-manasikāra*) is subsumed under four types of attention— namely, those of thorough knowledge of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*), resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*), observation (*mīmāṃsā*), and fruition (*phala*)—
and not merely under that attention of observation alone;
therefore it is said, "if one proceeds according to what remains, it should be understood accordingly."
Master Ki’s commentary states:
"This is explained with respect to the antidote that abandons; as for 'the remaining [antidotes] should be understood according to their respective applications,' there are two interpretations."
One interpretation states:
Only the attention that observes what has been abandoned and what has not yet been abandoned is subsumed under the attention of mere observation.
This is because it is explained in reference to the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) which serves as the antidote for abandoning the medium degree [of afflictions].

If one considers the remaining [stages], because they constitute the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the subsequent path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), they are likewise comprised within the three: the resolve that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-adhimokṣa*), the resolve of joy (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-adhimokṣa*), and [the resolve of analysis].
This is stated with reference to the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) for abandoning the inferior grade [of afflictions].
It is also subsumed under the mental application that is the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory stage;
therefore, it is said to be "according to what is appropriate. Second, it says:
Generally speaking, the four preceding types of attention (*manasikāra*) are subsumed as previously described;
however, they are explained here specifically in terms of their predominant meaning as the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) for abandoning the three grades [of afflictions].
This is based on the remaining sense of "endowment" (*samanvāgama*).
The two initial types of attention that accord with reality (*anuloma-manasikāra*) and the attention of joy in gathering (*saṃlikhita-manasikāra*) are subsumed under "observation" (*pratyavekṣaṇā*).
Since observation also extends to the subsequent stage of application (*prayoga*),
the attention that accords with purification (*viśuddhi-anukūla-manasikāra*) is likewise subsumed under observation.

The attention (*manasikāra*) that observes [the path] as abandoned or not yet abandoned is also subsumed under the stages of "joyful application" (*ratisaṃprayukta*) and "culmination of application" (*prayoganisthāphala*);
since the meaning is as previously explained, it is said to be "according to what is appropriate.
As for the attention of "forced exertion" (*balavāhana*), it is not subsumed under any of these.
The previously explained "forceful attention" (*balavāhana-manasikāra*) refers to the attention of one who has begun the practice but has not yet attained [higher] attention;

that is to say, it is the attention within the mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) which is being forcefully cultivated at the outset, as one has not yet attained the various attentions within the "not-yet-reached" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
Therefore, this forceful attention (*balavāhana-manasikāra*) is not included among the seven types of attention belonging to the meditative stages;
rather, it is subsumed under the types of attention that operate with interruption and effort, up to and including the "attention consisting of enjoyment" (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra*).
Jingyun: There is effortless application (*anābhoga-vṛtti*) and effortful application (*sābhoga-vṛtti*).
These two types of attention (*manasikāra*) comprise only the first four among the seven.
This means that because the resolve that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-adhimokṣa*) is free from the [resolve] of delighting in withdrawal (*pragraha*),
it is said to be "included up to the attention of delighting in withdrawal" (*pragrahā-manasikāra-saṃgṛhīta*). Jì (基) says:
There are twenty-eight types of attention with intervals,
which are subsumed under the "comprehension of characteristics" because they alternate with hearing and reflection.
Regarding the attention involving purposive effort,
twenty-eight [types] are taught;
it is subsumed under the next five [categories].
Because all [of these] involve the exertion of effort (*prayoga*).
Herein, the "attention of joy in gathering" (*saṃlikhitādhimokṣa-manasikāra*) is not mentioned briefly because it is common to the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*);
the observation regarding superior progress is the same.
Because one attains spontaneous operation through the attention of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*), it is called "spontaneous operation.
However, at that very moment, one is not yet spontaneously operative.
The twenty-eighth [verse] states that only the fruit of application is called "functioning without effort" (anābhoga-pravṛtti).
Among these twenty-eight, that which involves effort is called "uninterrupted" (nirantara),
because it is contrasted with what preceded it, which was "interrupted."
It is naturally termed "effortless" (*anābhoga*) because it is contrasted with the preceding stage that possesses effort through its forceful momentum.
Regarding the inclusion of the mental application of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-manasikāra*) within the mental application of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manasikāra*):
Because wisdom is predominantly generated by relying on the gate of initial cultivation, it is not excluded from the others.
Regarding that which is subsumed under internal attention and resolve:
it relies on the gate of internal objects immediately following the commencement [of practice].
It is not that they are not included by others. Regarding their inclusion within the mental application of observing the purification of hindrances (*pariśuddhy-āvaraṇa-manasikāra*):
this is based on the observation that the mental application of investigation observes whether afflictions have been abandoned or not, in accordance with the purification of hindrances.
It is not truly subsumed by them,
because it is not the correct path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Thus, the extensive mental orientations (*manasikāra*) are all not included therein.
The nirvana without abiding establishes the two benefits through compassion and wisdom and involves extensive practice;
it is not included among the seven [types of nirvana],
because those seven consist solely of self-benefit and do not involve extensive practice.
Regarding the inclusion within the ultimate fruit of the initial universal activity:
among the two types of universal activity mentioned previously,
the first— namely, that of the Buddha, the World-Honored One— is included within the fruit.

The second, "all-inclusive," refers to the mental engagements (*manasikāra*) of all bodhisattvas that consist of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) throughout the three vehicles (*yāna*) and the five fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*); these constitute their practice for self-benefit and are subsumed under seven categories.

Furthermore, the statement that "the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) serves as the condition for the [subsequent] transformation" is a reiterative explanation.
Regarding the phrase "included in what is established by others," this means that it is determined to have the hearing of another's voice and one's own mental attention as its conditions.
The first says:
Because they involve the thorough understanding of characteristics, commonality, hearing, and cultivation, they are subsumed under what is established by others.
The second says:
Although its nature consists solely of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*),
it is nevertheless categorized as "established by others" because it arises by externally relying on the teachings;
this is precisely the "attention for discerning characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedimanaskāra*) of the śrāvaka.

The attention that apprehends characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) through internal predominance and grasping takes as its condition only the previously accumulated provisions of merit and wisdom,
because there is no self-awakening [in this case].
This is precisely the attention that apprehends characteristics possessed by the *pratyekabuddhas* and all *bodhisattvas*.
The remaining six, such as resolve (*adhimokṣa*) and so forth, arise from the preceding mental attention (*manasikāra*) and the subsequent mental attention.

In the second part, which provides a detailed explanation of the distinctions among the objects of focus (*ālambana-viśeṣa*), there are two sections; first, [it explains] by means of the objects themselves as characteristics (*nimitta*).
Second, the specific clarification of the characteristics (*nimitta*).
This is because this object of focus (*ālambana*) is the objective sphere of all mental activities;
thus, it consists precisely of the characteristics that accompany meditative concentration and so forth.
In the section explaining the marks individually,
first the four marks and thirty-two marks are explained;
subsequently, the mutual inclusion of primary and secondary marks is explained.
The characteristic of the object of perception (*ālambana-nimitta*) refers to the essential characteristic of the entity that is the object of knowledge (*jñeya-vastu*).

The essence of discrimination (*vikalpa-svabhāva*) consists of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that act as the subject of cognition; the characteristic of discrimination (*vikalpa-nimitta*) is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the object of perception.
Because the concentrated mind takes these aspects of the sign as its object (*ālambana*). As for the causal sign (*nimitta*),
it refers to the requisites for concentration (*samādhi-sambhāra*),
namely the causes such as freedom from regret, joy, and bliss.
Regarding the four [factors] beginning with "not guarding the sense-doors," these are as previously explained.
First, not guarding the sense-doors.
Second, eating food beyond what is appropriate;
third, failing to constantly remain awake and diligently cultivate contemplative practice during the first and last watches of the night;
fourth, dwelling without clear comprehension.
This is explained in detail in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*.
The characteristics of sinking (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*) are as they are named.
The essence of attachment to signs has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its nature.
Or it may consist of the nature of all afflictions, such as craving, views, and doubt.
Regarding the thirty-two marks, what is the basis for the mark? It refers to the characteristic of the analytical essence (*vibhāga-svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
That is to say, the internal five aggregates and their seeds— namely,
the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) and the image-portion (nimitta-bhāga)— are called the "basis" (āśraya).
The six sense bases, such as form and so forth, are called the "objective aspect" (gocara-nimitta).
What are the characteristics of the arising of the mind?
There are two such characteristics:
first, the characteristic of the arising of all minds.
First, as stated immediately before, attention (*manasikāra*) is a single characteristic by which all minds arise, because it is due to attention that they do so.
Second, the characteristic of the arising of the eighth mind:
this refers to how, among the twelve links, the mind takes formations (*saṃskāra*) as its object and also arises taking name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as its object.
Regarding the phrase "What is the characteristic of its own nature? It refers to the own-nature of its own class," Ji states:
"The own-nature of its own class refers to the class of the five aggregates."
"Respective individual characteristics" refers to the fact that each aggregate (skandha) has its own distinct characteristic, such as the eye and so forth.
One interpretation states that "of their own kind" refers to the individual characteristics of the sense bases (āyatana).
"Individual" refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena.
Regarding this, for one who has already attained liberation but fails to apply the skillful means of abandonment, there is the contemplation of those possessed by craving and so forth. Jing says:
These ten pairs of fetters are associated with an undefiled mind;
that is to say, one observes a mind possessed of greed and so forth with a mind that is free from greed, hatred, and delusion, up to a mind that is already liberated.
For one who practices skillful means, "observing the concise, the inferior, and so forth" refers to this.
These ten pairs of fetters pertain to the defiled mind; that is to say, there is the mind with greed, hatred, and delusion; the contracted mind, and so forth, up to the unliberated mind;

the mind with greed and the mind without greed; the mind with hatred and the mind without hatred; the mind with delusion and the mind without delusion; the limited mind and the vast mind; the contracted mind and the expanded mind; the sunken mind and the uplifted mind; and so forth, up to the mind that should be cultivated and the mind that should not be cultivated, as well as the liberated mind and the unliberated mind.
Taiji said the same:
"Those who have left the household life are called 'renunciants' (niḥsṛta).
There are two categories of these."
One class of persons who do not cultivate the means for nirvāṇa contemplates the presence or absence of greed, the presence or absence of hatred, and the presence or absence of delusion.

Another class of persons who do cultivate the means for nirvāṇa contemplates the contracted mind, the expanded mind, the sinking mind, the uplifted mind, and so forth, up to the well-liberated mind and the poorly-liberated mind.
These are the characteristics of non-defilement; while the first three pairs of contemplations do not necessarily accord with the supramundane, the latter seven pairs do accord with the supramundane.
Ki further explains:
Alternatively, "cultivation" may refer to the application of skillful means in accordance with meditative concentration; it does not necessarily involve the application of skillful means,
nor is it necessarily supramundane.
Another explanation:

"One who does not cultivate skillful means" refers to one who has already attained liberation and no longer cultivates skillful means; therefore, such a person merely observes the three pairs of minds, beginning with those characterized by greed.
Regarding the cultivation of skillful means:

this refers to a person in training (*śaikṣa*) who contemplates the seven pairs of mental states, such as the concise and the detailed or the inferior and the superior, in order to accord with the renunciation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is the sign of light? It refers to that which serves as the antidote to darkness, or that which is the illumination of the Dharma.
In the preceding section on the food offering, three types of radiance were mentioned;
these are the first two.
Regarding "abiding in contemplation while seated," and so forth:
This is a separate explanation based on the three phrases of the sūtra. Jing says:
"Abiding" refers to the present.
One should sit facing the future;
or, while walking behind, one observes those ahead,
meaning that with each subsequent moment of the grasper, one contemplates each preceding moment.
The "grasping subject" (*grāhaka-dharma*) refers to the subsequent mind observing the preceding mind.
Master Ki further states that the future is called "sitting."
The present is called "dwelling," because it arises from the future and abides in the state of sitting and standing;
furthermore, this very present is also called "sitting."
The past is called "lying down" because one lies down after having first sat;
since the past has ceased, the designation "lying down" is established.
Regarding the phrase "how one enters the signs of meditative concentration by means of causes and conditions, etc.":
among the four preceding signs, the sign of what should be avoided is excluded;
these remaining three signs are conducive to entering meditative concentration.

Regarding the question, "What is the characteristic of emerging from meditative absorption (vyutthāna-lakṣaṇa), namely, those characteristics of the non-concentrated state (asamāhita-bhūmi) that are not subsumed under the essence of conceptualization (vikalpa)? Jì states:
"Although the essence of both concentrated and non-concentrated minds is common to conceptualization..."
The nature of this distracted mind, which is not subsumed by meditative concentration and belongs to the stage of non-concentration, is called the "mark of emergence.

Alternatively, the nature of discernment that is not subsumed by untainted (*anāsrava*) concentration and belongs to the stage of non-concentration is called the "mark of emerging from concentration."
Now, it is further explained:
the distracted mind is called "discrimination.
Because its essence is not subsumed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is termed the characteristic of the non-concentrated stage (*anirmitabhūmi*).
What is the characteristic of elicitation? It refers to the ability to elicit the path of the meanings of extensive texts and phrases through condensation.
This is the noble mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
By means of mastery over wisdom, speech, and sound, one incorporates all extensive texts and phrases into a single syllable.
By means of this single syllable, one encompasses the meaning of immeasurable words and phrases;
this universal reliance on meditative concentration to induce [realization] is termed the "characteristic of induction," extending even to the induction of all meritorious qualities.
The mutual inclusion [of these categories] can be understood.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā*, Fascicle Four, Part One, End.
